How Client1 interviews
What this primarily describes: How Client1 interviews — Start from your architecture, then drill whatever you named.

Definition

This interview is a coding drill from YOUR drawing, not a technology quiz. They hire Angular + .NET + SQL + AWS. You talk 90 seconds about the boxes you built; they then drill whatever you named. About 39 sessions in the PDF (2024–2026).
  • What it is: A hands-on full-stack coding interview. They start from your architecture, then JWT, Angular, .NET DI/SOLID, SQL, AWS. Behavioral comes later. Not a logo quiz.
  • How you use it: Interview 5 on every topic: what it is, where you used it, why, how you built it, what broke if you had not. Draw boxes. Stop when they interrupt.
  • Purpose / impact: Purpose: prove you can implement, not recite. Impact: name Neo4J / Kafka / Kubernetes you never used → they drill it and you fail. Stay on YOUR stack.
  • Two tracks: Core = Angular + .NET + SQL + AWS. Legacy also asks IIS, WebForms, and reading a stored procedure line by line. Angular lives on a separate URL → CORS + interceptor.

Interview — questions & answers

Q: What does this client actually hire for?

A: Hands-on full-stack: Angular, C#/.NET Core Web API, EF/SQL Server, JWT/OAuth, microservices, AWS (Gateway, ALB, ECS, S3). 100% coding, large team.

Q: How should I start every answer?

A: One sentence of what it is, then where I used it, why we chose it, how I built it, what broke if we had not.

Q: What gets people in trouble?

A: Naming Neo4J, Vue, WCF, or Kafka they never used. Interviewer validates previous-project usage. AWS answers that are only a service list.

Practice

  • Explain What it is with a project example.
  • Compare How you use it with an alternative.
  • Answer the Interview 5 for: Names the stack, typical order, and the Interview-5 rule without a definition dump
  • Speak the Interview 5 for C01 out loud (60 seconds).

Slide 2 of 21 · C1 — How they interview
Opening: architecture and R&R
What this primarily describes: Opening: architecture and R&R — Self intro, recent project, modules you owned, one design decision.

Definition

The opening is a 90-second flow you built, not a company org chart. Architecture = the click-to-database path. Roles = two features you coded. They then pick one box and drill.
  • What it is: A spoken drawing: Angular → interceptor → API → service → SQL → (queue/S3). Intro is 30 seconds (years, domain, stack). Not a slide of logos.
  • How you use it: Say the flow, then offer to go deeper on ONE box they pick. Roles and responsibilities = two modules you owned (endpoints, tables, one Angular screen) plus one production bug you found.
  • Purpose / impact: Purpose: prove you shipped code, not that the company has 40 services. Impact: “we use Kafka and Kubernetes” with no “I” → they cannot hire you. They interrupt — that is success.
  • Rating: They ask Angular / SQL / AWS out of 10. Defend with a story (I built interceptor + guards), not a 10. AWS honest: used vs studied.

Q: Explain your current project architecture.

A: SPA on its own host. Interceptor attaches JWT. .NET APIs behind a load balancer. SQL Server. I owned [module]. Auth is JWT bearer with refresh.

A: Design + code + SQL for [X]. Not 'I coordinated the team'. Name endpoints, tables, and one Angular screen.

Q: Where do you see yourself in 2 years? / rate yourself?

A: Deeper in this stack (AWS practical + LLD). Rating 7–8 on Angular/.NET/SQL with a story; AWS honest (used vs studied).

Slide 3 of 21 · C2 — Auth & Angular
JWT, OAuth, access vs refresh
What this primarily describes: JWT, OAuth, access vs refresh — Highest-frequency technical topic across core Client1 rounds.

Definition

A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a signed note in three pieces: header.payload.signature. Anyone can read it; only our key can prove it was not changed. Login usually gives two tokens: access (day-pass on every API) and refresh (spare key, only at /refresh). IdP = Identity Provider = login system. OIDC = OpenID Connect = who logged in. SSO = Single Sign-On = one IdP login for many apps.
  • What it is: JWT = signed claims, not encryption. Access = short Bearer on every API. Refresh = spare key at /refresh only. OAuth = permission. OIDC = who you are. IdP = Identity Provider.
  • How you use it: Login returns both. Interceptor sends access. API validates signature + exp + roles. On 401, refresh once, retry. Jobs use client credentials — never the user’s browser token.
  • Purpose / impact: Purpose: SPA + mobile share one API without cookies. Short access limits blast radius; refresh can be rotated/revoked. Impact: if access could mint access, a stolen XSS token lasts forever. Skip signature check → attacker sets role=Admin.
  • OAuth / OIDC / IdP: Four roles: End User, Angular (client), .NET API (resource server), IdP (Authorization Server). Angular = Code + PKCE. MVC = Code + secret. Hangfire = client credentials. Implicit = do not use.
⛶
Visual guide — OAuth vs OpenID Connect OAuth = permission to call an API (access token). OpenID Connect (OIDC) = proof of who logged in (id token). IdP = Identity Provider — the login system (Azure AD, Cognito, IdentityServer).

Visual guide — ID token vs access vs reference ID token = who you are (always a JWT, for the app). Access token = what you may call (for the API). Reference token = a random id, not a JWT — the API asks the IdP what it means.

ID token vs access vs reference – Visual Guide

Visual guide — Authorization Code vs Implicit Code flow = browser gets a short code, server swaps it for a token (safe). Implicit = token sits in the URL (old SPA style — do not use). Today Angular uses Code + PKCE.
⋮⋮

Authorization Code vs Implicit – Visual Guide

Visual guide — Access vs refresh, JWT claims Access token goes on every API call. Refresh token only asks for a new access token. JWT is signed, not encrypted — anyone can read it; they cannot change it without the key.

Visual guide — OAuth flows, OIDC, SPA vs job Angular (SPA = Single Page App) uses Code + PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange). .NET/Java server apps use Code + a secret. Hangfire uses client credentials. Implicit is old — do not use it. OIDC = OpenID Connect. IdP = Identity Provider.

OAuth flows, OIDC, SPA vs job – Visual Guide

Step-by-step (beginner friendly)

  • Step 1 — What JWT is, how you use it, why it matters
    Say this
    WhatA JWT (JSON Web Token) is a signed note in three pieces: header.payload.signature. Anyone can read the payload (Base64). Only our key can prove it was not changed. Login usually returns two tokens: access (day-pass) and refresh (spare key).
    How you use itInterceptor sends Authorization: Bearer <access> on every API. API checks signature + exp + roles. On 401, call /refresh once, retry. Jobs log in as an app (client credentials) — never copy the user’s browser token.
    PurposeOne login for Angular SPA + mobile against the same Web API, without cookies. Short access limits damage if stolen. Refresh can be rotated and revoked.
    ImpactSkip signature check → attacker sets role: Admin. Let access mint access → stolen XSS token lasts forever. No refresh rotation → stolen spare key prints day-passes forever.
    Without JWT BearerWith JWT Bearer (this stack)
    MVC cookie: browser sends it by itself. Awkward for mobile. CSRF risk.Interceptor attaches Bearer. Same API for SPA + mobile. XSS is the threat — short TTL + refresh rotation.

    Takeaway: JWT = signed, not secret. Access on every API. Refresh only at /refresh. API validates — Angular atob does not.

  • Step 2 — jwt.io sample (encoded vs decoded)

    A JWT is a signed note in three pieces joined by dots. jwt.io is a website that reads those pieces. Left = the token as it travels. Right = the same data as readable JSON. Green check = the signature matches the secret. Angular atob only reads — it does not check the signature.

    Encoded (jwt.io left). Three labeled parts: HEADER · PAYLOAD · SIGNATURE. Paste the full token into jwt.io:

    HEADER eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9
    PAYLOAD eyJzdWIiOiI0MiIsImVtYWlsIjoiYWRtaW5AY2xpZW50MS5sb2NhbCIsInJvbGUiOiJBZG1pbiIsImlzcyI6Imh0dHBzOi8vYXBpLmNsaWVudDEubG9jYWwiLCJhdWQiOiJjbGllbnQxLXNwYSIsImlhdCI6MTcxNzIwMDAwMCwiZXhwIjoxNzE3MjAzNjAwfQ
    SIGNATURE 3_6ChCvo613Glzef1pVOLjnXksOW8KO6e0MWeXgT8kY

    Full token (header.payload.signature):

    eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiI0MiIsImVtYWlsIjoiYWRtaW5AY2xpZW50MS5sb2NhbCIsInJvbGUiOiJBZG1pbiIsImlzcyI6Imh0dHBzOi8vYXBpLmNsaWVudDEubG9jYWwiLCJhdWQiOiJjbGllbnQxLXNwYSIsImlhdCI6MTcxNzIwMDAwMCwiZXhwIjoxNzE3MjAzNjAwfQ.3_6ChCvo613Glzef1pVOLjnXksOW8KO6e0MWeXgT8kY
    HEADER { "alg": "HS256", "typ": "JWT" }
    PAYLOAD { "sub": "42", "email": "admin@client1.local", "role": "Admin", "iss": "https://api.client1.local", "aud": "client1-spa", "iat": 1717200000, "exp": 1717203600 }
    VERIFY SIGNATURE HMACSHA256( base64Url(header) + "." + base64Url(payload), secret ) Demo secret: client1-demo-secret — paste it in jwt.io to see the signature valid. The API uses its real signing key. Decode ≠ verify.
    ClaimValueWhat it means
    alg / typHS256 / JWTHeader: HMAC-SHA256, this is a JWT. API must enforce the algorithm (do not trust alg: none).
    sub42Subject — the user id the API will treat as the caller.
    email / roleadmin@client1.local / AdminIdentity + role claim. [Authorize(Roles = "Admin")] reads role.
    iss / audapi.client1.local / client1-spaWho signed it, who may use it. ValidateIssuer + ValidateAudience.
    iat1717200000Issued-at: 2024-06-01 00:00 UTC (unix seconds).
    exp1717203600Expires 01:00 UTC (1 hour later). Past exp → 401. Server clock is source of truth.

    Takeaway: Anyone can decode the payload (it is Base64, not encryption). Only the holder of the signing key can produce a valid signature. UI may read exp for a countdown; the API still validates signature + exp + roles.

    What jwt.io shows, in order:

    1. Encoded (left): paste header.payload.signature. Colors = the three parts, not encryption.
    2. HEADER (right, pink): decoded JSON — alg + typ. Always readable.
    3. PAYLOAD (right, purple): decoded claims. Always readable. This is what Angular atob(token.split('.')[1]) sees.
    4. VERIFY SIGNATURE (right, blue): paste secret client1-demo-secret. Green check = HMAC of header.payload matches the third part. Red X = tampered payload, wrong secret, or truncated token.
    5. Experiment: change one character in the payload JSON on the right — encoded payload changes, signature goes red. That is tamper detection.
    6. jwt.io is a debugger. Production API uses ValidateIssuerSigningKey with the real key. A green check on jwt.io with the demo secret does not mean a stolen token is trusted by our API.
  • Step 3 — Four OAuth roles and IdP (Identity Provider)

    OAuth always has four players. IdP means Identity Provider — the login system. Same thing as Authorization Server.

    OAuth nameSimple nameIn this project
    Resource OwnerEnd user — youThe person who logs in and clicks Allow
    ClientThe app that asks for dataAngular SPA (or MVC). It never sees the password.
    Resource ServerWebsite / API that holds dataOur .NET Web API
    Authorization ServerIdP = Identity ProviderAzure AD, Cognito, IdentityServer, or Auth0

    IdP expansion: Identity Provider is the app that knows who you are. It shows the login page, checks the password (or SSO = Single Sign-On), and issues tokens. It is not Angular. It is not the orders API.

    Simple story: You click Login in Angular → Angular sends you to the IdP → you type password at Azure AD / IdentityServer → IdP gives Angular tokens → Angular calls the .NET API with the access token.

    Takeaway: If they say IdP, say “Identity Provider” out loud, then name yours. Map all four roles to your project. Open the visual guide OAuth 2 roles — IdP = Identity Provider.

  • Step 4 — ID token vs access token vs reference token

    Three different tokens. Do not mix them up.

    ID tokenAccess tokenReference token
    What it answersWho logged in?What may this caller do?A ticket number — look it up
    FormatAlways a JWTOften a JWT, not requiredNot a JWT — random id
    Who reads itThe client app (Angular)The API (Resource Server)API asks the IdP “what is this id?”
    aud (audience)The client id (the Angular app)The API name(s)—
    Typical claimsname, email, subscope, grant typeNothing inside — opaque

    Open the visual guide ID token vs access vs reference to see both JWTs decoded side by side.

    Takeaway: ID token = identity (OIDC). Access token = permission (OAuth). Reference token = “call me back to check.” Our Web API validates the access token, not the id token.

  • Step 5 — Why access cannot mint a new access token

    Access token = day-pass for APIs. Refresh token = spare key at the desk. The day-pass cannot print a new day-pass. If it could, a stolen token would last forever. XSS = Cross-Site Scripting — a script on our page can steal a token from browser storage.

    Access tokenRefresh token
    Sent onEvery API (Authorization: Bearer)Only /refresh (or token endpoint)
    LifetimeMinutes (15–60)Hours/days, rotated
    StorageMemory / session / localStorageHashed in SQL, or httpOnly cookie
    If stolenAttacker calls APIs until expAttacker could mint new access — so we rotate + revoke
    Can mint access?No — no refresh privilege in the JWTYes — that is its only job

    Analogy: hotel room key vs ID at the front desk. The room key opens the door; it does not print a new key. Front desk checks a different credential and can refuse.

    Takeaway: Short access + separate refresh limits blast radius. Login usually returns both. 401 → interceptor calls /refresh once → new access → retry.

  • Step 6 — Tampering: full explanation and code

    Anyone can read a JWT — it is encoded (Base64), not secret. Anyone can change role from User to Admin and re-encode. The API still says no, because the signature no longer matches. That check uses a key the attacker does not have.

    Original: HEADER . PAYLOAD(role=User) . SIG Attacker: HEADER . PAYLOAD(role=Admin) . SIG ← same SIG, new payload API: HMAC(HEADER + "." + NEW_PAYLOAD, key) != SIG → 401

    Full server code (this is what catches tamper and expiry):

    1builder.Services.AddAuthentication(JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
    2 .AddJwtBearer(o =>
    3 {
    4 o.TokenValidationParameters = new TokenValidationParameters
    5 {
    6 ValidateIssuer = true,
    7 ValidateAudience = true,
    8 ValidateLifetime = true, // exp → SecurityTokenExpiredException
    9 ValidateIssuerSigningKey = true, // tamper → SecurityTokenInvalidSignatureException
    10 ValidIssuer = "https://api.client1.local",
    11 ValidAudience = "client1-spa",
    12 IssuerSigningKey = new SymmetricSecurityKey(key)
    13 };
    14 });
    15[Authorize(Roles = "Admin")] // reads the role claim AFTER signature is valid

    What an attacker tries (and why it fails):

    var parts = accessJwt.Split('.'); var json = Encoding.UTF8.GetString(WebEncoders.Base64UrlDecode(parts[1])); var evil = json.Replace("User", "Admin"); // tamper the role claim var forged = parts[0] + "." + WebEncoders.Base64UrlEncode(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(evil)) + "." + parts[2]; // kept the OLD signature // forged still looks like header.payload.signature // JwtBearer: signature check fails → 401. Guards / atob never saw this request.

    Angular atob: useful to read exp for a countdown. It does not verify HMAC. Never authorize an admin screen from a decoded payload alone.

    Takeaway: Tamper = signature mismatch. Expiry = exp. Both are server 401s. The code editor on this slide is this pipeline.

  • Step 7 — Forms + cookie vs JWT (side by side)

    Old web apps keep you logged in with a cookie. Angular + mobile keep you logged in with a JWT on the Authorization header. Same idea (prove who you are), different envelope. Cookie = the browser sends it by itself. JWT = our interceptor attaches it.

    Forms auth + cookieJWT Bearer
    Typical appMVC / WebForms, same siteAngular SPA + mobile + same Web API
    LoginPOST username/password; server sets cookiePOST login API; returns access (+ refresh)
    Each requestBrowser sends cookie automaticallyInterceptor sets Authorization: Bearer
    CSRFMust use antiforgery tokensNo cookie for API → classic CSRF is weaker; XSS is the threat
    XSShttpOnly cookie cannot be read by JSToken in storage can be read by JS — short TTL + refresh rotation
    MobileAwkward (no browser cookie jar)Natural — store token in the app
    ServerOften session or cookie ticketStateless API (refresh store is the exception)
    HTTPSRequiredRequired

    Takeaway: Client1 is Angular + Web API + mobile-capable → JWT Bearer. Legacy IIS/WebForms track may still be cookie/forms. Do not say JWT is “more secure”; say it fits SPA + mobile.

  • Step 8 — Background jobs CAN authenticate (client credentials)

    A background job (Hangfire / timer) has no human and no refresh token. It still logs in — as an app, using client id + secret. That grant is called client credentials. Never copy a user's browser token into the job.

    User (Angular)Background job (Hangfire)
    Who logs in?Human at the IdP / login APINobody — the app authenticates
    GrantAuthorization Code + PKCE (or our login+refresh)Client credentials
    TokensUser access + refreshService access token only
    Where secret livesNot in the browserServer config / AWS secret / managed identity
    Never—Copy user's localStorage JWT into the job
    POST /connect/token grant_type=client_credentials client_id=hangfire-worker client_secret=*** → { "access_token": "<service JWT>", "expires_in": 3600 } HttpClient: Authorization: Bearer <service JWT> API [Authorize] — role/scope = worker, not Admin user

    Takeaway: Jobs do use JWT — a client-credentials access token. They do not use the user's refresh flow.

  • Step 9 — OAuth flows vs OIDC (SPA, .NET/Java, background job)

    OAuth 2.0 = permission (“this app may call these APIs”) — gives an access token. OIDC = OpenID Connect = “who logged in” — gives an id token. IdP = Identity Provider = the login system. SSO = Single Sign-On = one IdP login for many apps. JWT is only the token shape, not the protocol.

    Which flow: SPA (Single Page App, Angular) uses Authorization Code + PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) — no secret in the browser. .NET MVC / Java uses Authorization Code + a server secret. Hangfire uses client credentials. Implicit (token in the URL) is old — do not use it. Open the visual guide OAuth flows, OIDC, SPA vs job.

    Authorization CodeCode + PKCEImplicitHybridClient credentials
    Who.NET MVC / Java Spring (server has a secret)Angular SPA, mobileOld SPA (token in URL hash)Older OIDC (code + tokens at once)Hangfire / worker / daemon
    User present?Yes — browser loginYesYesYesNo
    Client secretYes, on the serverNo (public client)NoUsually yesYes, on the server
    Today?Yes for confidential appsYes — use this for SPADeprecated — do notRareYes — use this for jobs
    .NET MVC / Java SpringAngular SPABackground job
    FlowAuthorization Code (confidential)Authorization Code + PKCEClient credentials
    OIDC?Yes — cookie after id_tokenYes — login at IdP, API gets access JWTNo user — OAuth only
    API callCookie or BearerBearer access JWT via interceptorBearer service JWT

    Takeaway: SPA = Code+PKCE. Server web app (.NET or Java) = Code + secret. Job = client credentials. Implicit = no. OAuth + OIDC together because APIs and login are different problems.

  • Step 10 — JWT secure steps (important interview question)

    The library does not save you. Five locks: (1) sign it, (2) long key, (3) HTTPS, (4) hide the token from JavaScript, (5) stop CSRF. XSS = Cross-Site Scripting (a script on our page — not CSS). CSRF = Cross-Site Request Forgery (another site tricks the browser into sending our cookie). Open the visual guide JWT secure steps (interview).

    StepAttack if we skip itWhat we do
    1. Sign the tokenNo algorithm / alg: none — anyone can mint a JWT with role: Admin.Require HS256 or RS256. ValidateIssuerSigningKey = true. Never trust the alg header alone.
    2. Strong secret / keyA 6-character secret is brute-forced. HMAC-SHA256 needs a long key.At least 32 bytes (256-bit) for HS256. Do not use “password1”. RSA/EC: private key stays on the server.
    3. No port 80HTTP = packet sniff. The Bearer token is readable on the wire.HTTPS only (443). Redirect HTTP → HTTPS. HSTS in production.
    4. Storage vs XSSThe notes said “CSS” — they mean XSS (Cross-Site Scripting). A script can read localStorage / sessionStorage even on HTTPS.Prefer an httpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookie. JavaScript cannot read httpOnly. XSS does not “hack CSS.”
    5. CSRF fingerprintThe browser auto-sends cookies. A malicious site can trigger a request (CSRF) even with HTTPS + httpOnly.Antiforgery / fingerprint: put the same random value in (1) an httpOnly cookie and (2) a JWT claim. API accepts only if they match. Same idea as MVC antiforgery tokens.

    Fingerprint (say this in the interview):

    Login: fp = random 32 bytes Set-Cookie: __Host-fp=fp; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict JWT claim: "fp": sha256(fp) Each API: cookieFp = Request.Cookies["__Host-fp"] jwtFp = User.FindFirst("fp")?.Value if (sha256(cookieFp) != jwtFp) return 401; // CSRF — cookie came without our JWT

    Takeaway: Sign → long key → HTTPS → httpOnly → match fingerprint. Skip any one lock and the “right library” still loses. XSS ≠ CSS. Cookie stops XSS-read; CSRF still needs the fingerprint.

Interview — questions & answers

Q: Difference between access token and refresh token? Do we get both at login? If we have access, why not use it to get a new access token?

A: Usually both at login. Access = short day-pass on every API (Bearer). Refresh = spare key, used only at /refresh, stored hashed (or httpOnly cookie), rotated and revocable. If access could mint access, a stolen XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) token would last forever — that is why refresh exists.

Q: How do you know the payload was not tampered? How do you know access expired?

A: Payload is Base64url — anyone can edit role to Admin and re-encode. Tamper is caught because HMACSHA256(header.payload, server key) no longer matches the signature → JwtBearer throws SecurityTokenInvalidSignatureException → 401. Expiry is the exp claim (ValidateLifetime) → SecurityTokenExpiredException → 401. Angular atob is not this check.

Q: JWT vs traditional cookie/form auth? Web + mobile?

A: Forms + cookie: browser posts username/password, server sets a cookie (often httpOnly). Same-site MVC/WebForms. Need antiforgery because the browser sends cookies by itself. JWT Bearer: interceptor sets Authorization header. Same Web API for Angular SPA (Single Page App) and mobile. Threat is XSS (Cross-Site Scripting), not classic CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery). Both need HTTPS and a short lifetime.

Q: What if there is no refresh token (async / background job)? Can we still authenticate the job?

A: Yes — background jobs CAN and SHOULD authenticate. Use OAuth client credentials (client id + secret, or AWS/Azure managed identity) to get a service access token. That is not a user refresh flow. Never copy a user's localStorage JWT into Hangfire.

Q: What does jwt.io show? Is decoding the same as validating?

A: Left = encoded HEADER.PAYLOAD.SIGNATURE (pink/purple/blue). Right HEADER JSON, PAYLOAD JSON, then VERIFY SIGNATURE. Paste the secret to see a green check (HMAC matches). Change one payload character and it goes red. Decoding is always possible; the green check is verification. The API does verification with its real key — jwt.io is a debugger, not the API.

Q: OAuth vs OpenID Connect? Which flow for Angular vs .NET/Java vs a background job?

A: OAuth 2.0 = permission to call APIs (access token). OIDC = OpenID Connect = who logged in (id token). IdP = Identity Provider = login system. SPA (Single Page App, Angular) = Authorization Code + PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange — no secret in the browser). .NET MVC / Java = Authorization Code + a server secret. Background job = client credentials. Implicit (token in the URL) is old — do not use it.

Q: What is an IdP? What are the four OAuth roles?

A: IdP = Identity Provider. Same as Authorization Server — the login system (Azure AD, Cognito, IdentityServer, Auth0). Four roles: Resource Owner = End User (you). Resource Server = Website/API (our .NET API). Client = Angular web/MVC. Authorization Server = the IdP.

Q: ID token vs access token vs reference token?

A: ID token = who you are (always a JWT, for the app). Access token = what APIs you may call (for the API). Reference token = a random ticket number, not a JWT; the API asks the IdP (Identity Provider) what it means.

Q: How do you harden JWT so it is not hacked even with the right library?

A: Five locks: (1) sign it — never alg:none. (2) long key, at least 32 bytes. (3) HTTPS only. (4) XSS = Cross-Site Scripting (not CSS) can read localStorage; prefer httpOnly cookie. (5) CSRF = Cross-Site Request Forgery — match an antiforgery fingerprint in the JWT and the cookie.

Slide 4 of 21 · C2 — Auth & Angular
Interceptor, token storage, route guards
What this primarily describes: Interceptor, token storage, route guards — How the SPA attaches JWT, where it lives, how admin pages are blocked.

Definition

An interceptor is a checkpoint in Angular’s HttpClient pipeline — middleware for HTTP. Every API call from the app passes through it on the way out, and the response comes back through it. You write it once; Angular runs it. Screens never call it. On one page visit: route guard (may I open this page?) → constructor (DI) → ngOnInit (HTTP) → interceptor (stamp the request) → API.
  • What it is: Not a component, not a route, not a guard. It is HttpClient middleware: a class or function with intercept(req, next). Think of a post-office stamp — every letter leaving the app goes through that one stamp.
  • How you use it: Register once in app config: { provide: HTTP_INTERCEPTORS, useClass: AuthInterceptor, multi: true } (or withInterceptors([authInterceptor])). After that, this.http.get('/orders') is enough. You do not call intercept() from a screen.
  • Purpose / impact: Purpose: one place for jobs that belong on every HTTP call — attach Authorization: Bearer, refresh once on 401, log, add a correlation id. Impact: without it, every screen copies the header; miss one call → API 401. Forget to register it → user looks logged in, every API still 401s. With it, login once and every HttpClient call carries the token.
  • Guards vs interceptor: Guard = may I open this Angular route? (UX, before the component). Interceptor = stamp HTTP with the token (on the wire). Neither is the real lock — the API [Authorize] is. Storage: localStorage survives refresh; sessionStorage dies with the tab; XSS can read both.

Step-by-step (beginner friendly)

  • Step 1 — What an interceptor is, how you use it, why it matters

    Open the visual guide Angular URL vs API interceptors after you read this. Three scenarios: opening an Angular URL (guard only), logged-in API call (Auth + Logging + ErrorInterceptor), and no token (guard blocks the page; interceptor does not invent a Bearer — API 401).

    Say this
    WhatA checkpoint in the HttpClient pipeline. Every outgoing API call (and its response) goes through it. Same idea as .NET middleware / DelegatingHandler, but on the Angular side.
    How you use it1) Write intercept(req, next). 2) Register it once in app config. 3) Stop. Screens call this.api.list() as usual — Angular runs the interceptor. You clone the request (it is frozen); you never edit the original.
    PurposeJobs that belong on every HTTP call, not on one screen: attach JWT, refresh on 401, logging, correlation id. Auth interceptor: read token from storage → req.clone({ setHeaders: { Authorization: 'Bearer …' } }) → next.handle(…). On 401, call /refresh once, retry the original call.
    ImpactOne place to change auth for the whole SPA. Forget to register → login “works” but every API returns 401. Copy the header on each screen → miss one screen, that screen 401s. Guard does not replace this: the guard only hides a route; the interceptor stamps the HTTP the API actually sees.
    Without interceptorWith interceptor (what we do)
    this.http.get('/orders', { headers: { Authorization: 'Bearer ' + token } })
    Repeat on users, reports, admin… miss one → 401.    		Register AuthInterceptor once.
    Then every screen: this.http.get('/orders'). Token is added in the middle.

    Not the interceptor: a route guard (page yes/no, before the component exists). A constructor. [Authorize] on the API (the real lock).

    Takeaway: Interceptor = stamp every HTTP call in one place. Register once. Components never call it. Missing stamp → 401. Missing API check → anyone with a URL can still hit the server.

  • Step 2 — Angular lifecycle: route, token, interceptor

    One visit to a page, in order. Open the visual guide Angular lifecycle — route, token, interceptor.

    WhenWhat Angular doesToken / interceptor / route
    1. Bootstrapmain.ts starts the appToken is already in storage from login (or missing)
    2. RouterMatches the URL, e.g. /adminPicks the route and its canActivate guard
    3. Route guardcanActivate runs before the component existsReads the token (and role) from storage / AuthService. No token → login. Guard does not call the interceptor
    4. constructorAngular creates the component and injects servicesDI only. @Input is not set. Do not call HTTP here
    5. ngOnInitInputs are ready. Screen loads dataComponent calls this.api.list(). That is HttpClient
    6. InterceptorHttpClient pipeline, registered once as HTTP_INTERCEPTORSReads the same token, clones the request, sets Authorization: Bearer. On 401, refresh once
    7. API.NET JwtBearer + [Authorize]The real lock. A hidden Angular route is not security
    8. ngOnDestroyUser leaves the screenUnsubscribe. Token stays until logout clears storage

    Simple story: Login writes the token. Opening /admin — the route guard checks it first. The page then starts — constructor (DI), then ngOnInit (HTTP). The interceptor sticks the token on that HTTP call. The API still checks it.

    Takeaway: Guard = may I open this route? Interceptor = attach the token to HTTP. ngOnInit = load data. API = real lock. constructor is not for HTTP.

  • Step 3 — What it is (before/after)

    Not a component, not a route, not a guard. It is HttpClient middleware: a class or function with intercept(req, next). Think of a post-office stamp — every letter leaving the app goes through that one stamp.

    ❌ Before
    // BEFORE — Users cannot open /admin because of canActivate.
    ✔ After
    // AFTER — Guard for UX. API [Authorize(Roles = "Admin")] so a crafted HTTP call still 403s.

  • Step 4 — How you use it (before/after)

  • Step 7 — Step — From Angular.dev, Auth0, and Stack Overflow

    Our simple story stays. Open Angular URL vs API interceptors first (URL vs logged-in API vs no token), then angular.dev — lifecycle execution order. Then the visual guide From Angular.dev, Auth0, Stack Overflow.

    1. Interceptors — angular.dev / interceptors

    HttpClient middleware. Used for retry, cache, logging, and authentication — so each screen does not do it. Many interceptors form a chain: each one sees the request, then calls next. The response walks back the same chain. You must clone the request (it is immutable). Angular recommends a functional interceptor today:

    export const authInterceptor: HttpInterceptorFn = (req, next) => { const token = inject(AuthService).accessToken; const authReq = token ? req.clone({ setHeaders: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } }) : req; return next(authReq); }; provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([authInterceptor]));

    Older projects (still fine to name): class + { provide: HTTP_INTERCEPTORS, useClass: AuthInterceptor, multi: true }. Same clone + Bearer idea. Docs: functional has more predictable order; class-based “may be phased out.”

    2. Route guards — angular.dev / route-guards

    Official warning, quote: Never rely on client-side guards as the sole source of access control. JavaScript in the browser can be changed. Always authorize on the server too.

    GuardQuestion it answers
    canActivateMay this user open this route? (login / role)
    canActivateChildSame check for every child under a parent
    canDeactivateMay they leave? (unsaved form)
    canMatchDoes this route even match? (feature flag) — false tries the next route

    Return true / false, or a UrlTree to redirect. Docs: if you need login, return the UrlTree — do not return false and then router.navigate.

    export const authGuard: CanActivateFn = (route, state) => { const auth = inject(AuthService); const router = inject(Router); return auth.isAuthenticated() ? true : router.createUrlTree(['/login'], { queryParams: { returnUrl: state.url } }); };

    3. constructor vs ngOnInit — Stack Overflow (1,545 score, ~894k views) + angular.dev / lifecycle

    Accepted answer: constructor = JavaScript new + DI. ngOnInit = Angular is done creating the component; bindings are ready. “Constructor should only initialize class members / DI. ngOnInit is where you start.” Official table: ngOnInit runs once after inputs are set. First ngOnChanges (if any) runs before ngOnInit. @Input is not safe in the constructor. Call HTTP in ngOnInit — that is when the interceptor runs for that screen.

    4. Token storage — Auth0 Token Storage

    StoreAuth0 / OWASP viewWhat we say
    Memory / Web WorkerMost secure for a SPALost on refresh — Auth0 SDK default
    localStorageXSS can read it (any script, including a bad npm package)Nice UX; not a vault; short TTL
    httpOnly cookieJS cannot steal it; CSRF is the other riskSameSite + fingerprint if we use cookies

    Takeaway: Cite Angular.dev for chain + “guard is not the lock,” Stack Overflow for constructor vs ngOnInit, Auth0 for “memory > localStorage.” Our simple order is unchanged: guard → constructor → ngOnInit → interceptor → API.

Interview — questions & answers

Q: Walk Angular lifecycle for a page that needs JWT. Where do route, token, and interceptor sit?

A: Bootstrap the app. Router matches /admin. canActivate reads the token (and role) from storage — if missing, go to login; the component is not created yet. constructor only injects services. ngOnInit calls the service. HttpClient runs the interceptor, which clones the request and sets Authorization: Bearer. The API [Authorize] is the real lock. ngOnDestroy unsubscribes; logout clears the token.

Q: Purpose of interceptor? How many in your project? How does the request know about it?

A: It is HttpClient middleware — a checkpoint every HTTP call passes through. Purpose: do the same job in one place instead of on every screen. I used two: auth (clone the request, set Authorization: Bearer, on 401 refresh once and retry) and error (toast / log). The request knows because we register it once with HTTP_INTERCEPTORS (multi: true) or withInterceptors. HttpClient runs the chain; components never call intercept(). Without it, miss one header and the API 401s. It is not a guard and not a component hook.

Q: constructor vs ngOnInit — which one loads data with the token?

A: constructor is DI only — @Input is not set, do not call HTTP there. ngOnInit is where I call the service. The interceptor still attaches the token either way, but loading in ngOnInit is the lifecycle they expect.

Q: Where do you store the token? Why not sessionStorage?

A: We used localStorage so refresh of the SPA keeps the session. sessionStorage is better if you want tab isolation. I would not call either 'secure' — short TTL + HTTPS + server validation. Guard and interceptor both read the same store.

Q: Dashboard: admin sees all, user sees subset. How do you set the Angular page?

A: Route guard for /admin/*. API returns data filtered by role. Never trust hidden buttons as security.

Q: How do you handle access expiry without breaking the current operation?

A: Interceptor catches 401, queues the original request, calls /refresh, retries once. User stays on the same screen if refresh succeeds.

Q: Class interceptor vs functional interceptor?

A: Same job. Angular.dev now recommends a function (HttpInterceptorFn) registered with provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([authInterceptor])). Older Client1-style code uses a class + HTTP_INTERCEPTORS multi: true. Either way: clone the request, set Bearer, do not mutate the original.

Q: Auth0 / OWASP — is localStorage OK for the JWT?

A: Auth0 says browser memory (Web Worker / closure) is the most secure. localStorage survives refresh but XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) can steal it. I would say: we used localStorage for UX; it is not a vault; short TTL + HTTPS + API validation. Stronger: access in memory, refresh in httpOnly cookie.

Q: angular.dev — can I return false from canActivate and then navigate to login?

A: No. Docs say return a UrlTree or RedirectCommand to redirect. Do not return false and then call router.navigate. And never treat the guard as the only lock — always [Authorize] on the API.

Angular: pass data between components
What this primarily describes: Angular: pass data between components — 1 Properties · 2 Emitter · 3 RxJS · 4 Route.

Definition

Four ways to pass data. That is the whole slide. 1. Properties / fields = @Input (parent → child). 2. Emitter = @Output + EventEmitter (child → parent). 3. RxJS = shared service + Subject / BehaviorSubject (no parent-child). 4. Route = id on the URL (or router state) when you navigate. Do not inject the parent. Do not put a token in the query string.
  • 1. Properties / fields: Actual: parent sets a field on the child. Simple: @Input() user. Template: [user]="row". Down only.
  • 2. Emitter: Actual: child raises an event the parent listens to. Simple: @Output() saved = new EventEmitter(). Template: (saved)="reload()". Up only.
  • 3. RxJS: Actual: a root service pushes values; any screen subscribes. Simple: BehaviorSubject for last value (selected id, current user). Siblings / other module — no @Input.
  • 4. Route: Actual: navigation carries an id, not the whole row. Simple: /orders/42 or router state. Payload stays in the RxJS service. Never token/SSN in query string.

Interview — questions & answers

Q: How do you pass data between Angular components?

A: Four ways. 1 Properties: @Input parent to child. 2 Emitter: @Output EventEmitter child to parent. 3 RxJS: root service + BehaviorSubject when there is no parent-child. 4 Route: pass the id when you navigate. Not the parent injected, not a token in the URL.

Q: Standalone / no parent-child?

A: Number 3 — RxJS. A shared service. BehaviorSubject if a late screen still needs the last value.

Q: Users module to facility module?

A: Still 3 — same root service. Or 4 — navigate with the id. Lazy modules should not import each other just to pass a row.

RxJS: Observable, Promise, Subject
What this primarily describes: RxJS: Observable, Promise, Subject — Observable vs Promise, Subject vs BehaviorSubject, parallel APIs, retry.

Definition

RxJS is how Angular handles values over time. Observable = a stream (starts when you subscribe; you can cancel). Promise = one result (starts now; cannot cancel). Subject = you push the values. HttpClient returns an Observable — that is why we unsubscribe.
  • What it is: Observable = lazy stream, cancel with unsubscribe. Promise = one shot, eager. Subject = multicast you control. BehaviorSubject = Subject that remembers the last value (current user).
  • How you use it: HttpClient: subscribe in ngOnInit, unsubscribe in ngOnDestroy (or takeUntilDestroyed). Parallel HTTP: forkJoin. Last-known user: BehaviorSubject. Retry GET in the interceptor — not POST that charges a card.
  • Purpose / impact: Purpose: cancel leftover HTTP when the user leaves the page; share the logged-in user with late screens. Impact: Promise-only → cannot cancel, leaks after destroy. Subject for current user → a late subscriber sees nothing. Retry POST → double charge.
  • Parallel: forkJoin({ users, sites }) waits for all. One failure fails the group. Independent calls; not nested subscribe.
⛶
Visual guide — RxJS Observable Promise Subject Observable = many values over time. Promise = one value. Subject = you push the values.

    Say this
    WhatAn Observable is a stream of values over time. It starts when you subscribe. You can unsubscribe (cancel). A Promise is one value and starts immediately. HttpClient returns an Observable.
    How you use itCall the service in ngOnInit. Pipe takeUntilDestroyed(). Use BehaviorSubject for “current user” so a late screen still gets the last login. Parallel loads: forkJoin.
    PurposeCancel HTTP when the user leaves. Retry GET safely. Share last-known state without a parent-child template.
    ImpactNo unsubscribe → requests finish after destroy and write to a dead screen. Subject (not Behavior) for user → late subscriber is empty. Retry a payment POST → charged twice.
    WithoutWith
    fetch().then() in the component, no unsubscribethis.api.get().pipe(takeUntilDestroyed()).subscribe()

    Takeaway: HTTP is Observable so we can cancel. BehaviorSubject for last user. forkJoin for parallel. Retry GET only.

Interview — questions & answers

Q: Observable vs Promise?

A: Promise: one result, starts now. Observable: stream, starts on subscribe, can unsubscribe. HTTP in Angular is Observable.

Q: Subject vs BehaviorSubject?

A: BehaviorSubject has a current value; new subscribers get it immediately. Use for 'logged-in user'. Subject is fire-and-forget events.

Q: Call multiple APIs in parallel and shape the result?

A: forkJoin({ users: this.u.get(), sites: this.s.get() }).subscribe(x => this.vm = map(x)).

DI lifetimes: Singleton, Scoped, Transient
What this primarily describes: DI lifetimes: Singleton, Scoped, Transient — Highest-frequency .NET drill — they give a scenario and ask which lifetime.

Definition

DI (Dependency Injection) is the container constructing objects for you — you do not new a DbContext in the controller. Lifetime = how long that object lives. Transient = every resolve. Scoped = this HTTP request. Singleton = the whole app. They give a scenario and ask which lifetime — and why the others are wrong.
  • What it is: MS.DI in Program.cs. Transient = brand-new every time (stateless helper). Scoped = one per HTTP request (DbContext, Unit of Work). Singleton = one per process (cache, settings). Not “shared to two browsers.”
  • How you use it: AddDbContext (Scoped by default). AddScoped<IUnitOfWork, UnitOfWork>. AddSingleton<IMemoryCache>. Constructor injection: OrdersController(IUnitOfWork uow).
  • Purpose / impact: Purpose: one change-tracker and one transaction per request; swap SQL in tests. Impact: DbContext as Singleton → leaked tracker, two users share one context, threading bugs. Scoped inside Singleton (“captive”) → the first request’s DbContext lives forever.
  • Captive dependency: A Singleton must not hold a Scoped DbContext. If it does, every later request uses the first user’s database context. Fix: do not inject Scoped into Singleton.
⛶
Visual guide — DI lifetimes Transient = new each time. Scoped = once per HTTP request (DbContext). Singleton = once per app.

Picks Scoped for DbContext and explains captive dependency
Interview — questions & answers

Q: Which lifetime is suitable for DataSource / DbContext?

A: Scoped. One context per HTTP request. Singleton would share tracker across users. Transient would break a Unit of Work that needs one context.

Q: How do you configure DI in .NET Core? Other containers?

A: builder.Services.AddScoped(). Built-in MS.DI. Autofac if the project used modules — only if I used it.

Q: Singleton across two browsers?

A: No. Each browser is a client. Server Singleton is one object per app process (or per replica). User state stays in the token or SQL.

SOLID — especially Open/Closed
What this primarily describes: SOLID — especially Open/Closed — Very frequently asked with 'how in your class' and dynamic polymorphism.

Definition

SOLID is five design rules. Walk them in order. S = one class, one job. O = add a new class, do not keep editing the old if/else. L = a child must not surprise callers of the parent. I = small interfaces — do not force unused methods. D = depend on a contract (IEmailClient), not new SmtpClient() inside EmailNotifier. They drill O hardest: name the if you replaced in YOUR class. sealed is not OCP.
  • S — Single responsibility: Actual: a class should have only one reason to change. Simple: one class, one job. Split the god Notifier: EmailNotifier only emails, SmsNotifier only texts, NotificationLog only logs. No interface yet.
  • O — Open/Closed: Actual: open for extension, closed for modification. Simple: add SlackNotifier (new file); do not reopen EmailNotifier or OrderNotify. How: interface or abstract class (the plug) + polymorphism + DI (IEnumerable<INotifier> + one AddTransient). sealed is not OCP.
  • L — Liskov substitution: Actual: a subtype must replace the parent without breaking the caller. Simple: every INotifier.SendAsync must send or no-op — never throw NotImplemented.
  • I — Interface segregation: Actual: do not force clients to depend on methods they do not use. Simple: ExportHistory is not on INotifier. History is INotificationHistory.
  • D — Dependency inversion: Actual: depend on abstractions, not details. Simple: inject IEmailClient. Do not new SmtpClient() inside EmailNotifier.
⛶
Visual guide — SOLID Open Closed O = interface or abstract (plug) + DI (register Slack). Not a bigger if. sealed is not OCP.

⛶

SOLID — five letters, before and after – Visual Guide

Step-by-step (beginner friendly)

  • Step 1 — S — Single responsibility
    KindDefinition
    ActualA class should have only one reason to change. (Robert C. Martin)
    SimpleOne class, one job. Change SMTP → open EmailNotifier only. Change the log path → open NotificationLog only.

    Start with notification only. One Notifier formats, logs, sends email, and sends SMS. Change SMTP → you open this class. Change the log path → you open the same class. That is more than one reason to change.

    How S solves it: one job per class. EmailNotifier only emails. SmsNotifier only texts. NotificationLog only logs. No interface yet — that plug comes at O. We still pick Email vs Sms with if. Last lines of each sample: they call Notifier.Notify("Email", msg) before, and OrderNotify.Send("Email", msg) after.

    ❌ Before — one class, four jobs
    1public class Message {
    2 public string To { get; set; }
    3 public string Text { get; set; }
    4}
    5 
    6public class Notifier {
    7 public void Notify(string type, Message m) {
    8 var html = "<p>" + m.Text + "</p>";
    9 File.AppendAllText("notify.log", m.To + " " + m.Text);
    10 if (type == "Email") {
    11 using var smtp = new SmtpClient("smtp.company.com");
    12 smtp.Send("noreply@co.com", m.To, "Notice", html);
    13 }
    14 else if (type == "Sms") {
    15 Twilio.Send(m.To, m.Text);
    16 }
    17 }
    18}
    19 
    20// How they call it
    21var msg = new Message { To = "a@co.com", Text = "Order 42 shipped" };
    22new Notifier().Notify("Email", msg);
    23new Notifier().Notify("Sms", msg);
    ✔ After — one job each, still if/else
    1public class Message {
    2 public string To { get; set; }
    3 public string Text { get; set; }
    4}
    5 
    6public class NotificationLog {
    7 public void Write(Message m) {
    8 File.AppendAllText("notify.log",
    9 m.To + " " + m.Text + Environment.NewLine);
    10 }
    11}
    12 
    13public class EmailNotifier {
    14 public void Send(Message m) {
    15 using var smtp = new SmtpClient("smtp.company.com");
    16 smtp.Send("noreply@co.com", m.To, "Notice", m.Text);
    17 }
    18}
    19 
    20public class SmsNotifier {
    21 public void Send(Message m) {
    22 Twilio.Send(m.To, m.Text);
    23 }
    24}
    25 
    26public class OrderNotify {
    27 NotificationLog _log = new NotificationLog();
    28 public void Send(string type, Message m) {
    29 _log.Write(m);
    30 if (type == "Email") new EmailNotifier().Send(m);
    31 else if (type == "Sms") new SmsNotifier().Send(m);
    32 }
    33}
    34 
    35// How they call it — same Message, new coordinator
    36var msg = new Message { To = "a@co.com", Text = "Order 42 shipped" };
    37new OrderNotify().Send("Email", msg);
    38new OrderNotify().Send("Sms", msg);

    Takeaway: SMTP change now lives in EmailNotifier. OrderNotify still has if type — that is the next letter, not S.

  • Step 2 — O — Open/Closed
    KindDefinition
    ActualSoftware entities (classes, modules, functions) should be open for extension, but closed for modification. (Bertrand Meyer / Robert C. Martin)
    SimpleAdd Slack as a new class. Do not keep editing OrderNotify or EmailNotifier. sealed is not this.

    Same notification. Product wants Slack. After S, Slack means another else if in OrderNotify.Send — that working dispatcher is not closed.

    WordMeansIn this story
    ClosedDo not reopen working files to add Slack.EmailNotifier, SmsNotifier, and OrderNotify.Send stay as they are.
    OpenYou can add Slack anyway.New file SlackNotifier + one DI line.
    InterfaceThe plug shape — not the word “open.”INotifier.SendAsync. Email, Sms, Slack all fit. The caller never writes if type ==.
    Concept that achieves OWhat it doesIn this story
    Interface (usual in .NET)Shared contract. New types plug in. No shared code in the base.INotifier with SendAsync. Email / Sms / Slack each implement it.
    Abstract class (when they share code)Same idea — a base you extend — plus shared fields or helper methods.Use if every notifier must log first: abstract class NotifierBase with a concrete WriteLog and abstract SendAsync. Slack still = new subclass, not a new else if.
    PolymorphismCaller talks to the base. Runtime picks Email vs Slack.foreach (var x in _n) await x.SendAsync(m); — no if type.
    Dependency injectionThe closed class does not new Slack. The container hands in every INotifier.Ctor: OrderNotify(IEnumerable<INotifier> n). Slack = AddTransient<INotifier, SlackNotifier>() — that is the one new line, not an edit to Send.

    How O solves it: S split the jobs but still used if. O adds the plug (INotifier here; abstract class if they share code) and DI so OrderNotify stays closed. Interface / abstract = what you extend. DI = how the new class gets in without editing the caller. sealed only blocks inheritance — that is not this “closed.” D (later) is a second plug: IEmailClient inside EmailNotifier, not the channel list.

    ❌ Before — OrderNotify from S, not closed
    1public class OrderNotify {
    2 NotificationLog _log = new NotificationLog();
    3 public void Send(string type, Message m) {
    4 _log.Write(m);
    5 if (type == "Email") new EmailNotifier().Send(m);
    6 else if (type == "Sms") new SmsNotifier().Send(m);
    7 // Slack? edit THIS method again
    8 }
    9}
    10 
    11// How they call it — still a type string
    12var msg = new Message { To = "a@co.com", Text = "Order 42 shipped" };
    13new OrderNotify().Send("Email", msg);
    14new OrderNotify().Send("Sms", msg);
    15// new OrderNotify().Send("Slack", msg); // does nothing until you edit Send
    ✔ After — closed caller + new Slack class
    1public interface INotifier { // plug (or abstract class)
    2 Task SendAsync(Message m);
    3}
    4 
    5public class EmailNotifier : INotifier {
    6 public Task SendAsync(Message m) {
    7 using var smtp = new SmtpClient("smtp.company.com");
    8 smtp.Send("noreply@co.com", m.To, "Notice", m.Text);
    9 return Task.CompletedTask;
    10 }
    11}
    12 
    13public class SmsNotifier : INotifier {
    14 public Task SendAsync(Message m) {
    15 Twilio.Send(m.To, m.Text);
    16 return Task.CompletedTask;
    17 }
    18}
    19 
    20public class SlackNotifier : INotifier { // NEW FILE
    21 public Task SendAsync(Message m) {
    22 Slack.Post(m.To, m.Text);
    23 return Task.CompletedTask;
    24 }
    25}
    26 
    27public class OrderNotify { // CLOSED — no if type
    28 private readonly IEnumerable<INotifier> _n;
    29 private readonly NotificationLog _log;
    30 public OrderNotify(IEnumerable<INotifier> n, NotificationLog log) {
    31 _n = n; _log = log;
    32 }
    33 public async Task Send(Message m) {
    34 _log.Write(m);
    35 foreach (var x in _n) await x.SendAsync(m);
    36 }
    37}
    38 
    39builder.Services.AddTransient<INotifier, EmailNotifier>();
    40builder.Services.AddTransient<INotifier, SmsNotifier>();
    41builder.Services.AddTransient<INotifier, SlackNotifier>();
    42builder.Services.AddTransient<NotificationLog>();
    43builder.Services.AddTransient<OrderNotify>();
    44 
    45// How they call it — controller / PlaceOrder (no "Email"/"Sms" string)
    46public class OrdersController {
    47 private readonly OrderNotify _notify;
    48 public OrdersController(OrderNotify notify) { _notify = notify; }
    49 public async Task Place(Message m) {
    50 await _notify.Send(m); // Email + Sms + Slack all run
    51 }
    52}

    Takeaway: Closed = files you do not edit. Open = new class. Achieved with interface or abstract class (plug) + DI (register Slack). sealed ≠ OCP.

  • Step 3 — L — Liskov substitution
    KindDefinition
    ActualIf S is a subtype of T, objects of type T may be replaced with objects of type S without breaking the caller. (Barbara Liskov)
    SimpleSlackNotifier must be usable wherever INotifier is. SendAsync must not throw. A no-op is allowed; a fake throw is not.

    Same INotifier. Staging turns Slack off. Someone “implements” Slack by throwing. OrderNotify still calls every notifier. Email worked; the whole Send now blows up. Slack cannot stand in for INotifier.

    How L solves it: SendAsync must behave like Email — finish without throwing. If Slack is off, return a completed task (no-op). Do not lie with NotImplementedException.

    ❌ Before — Slack is not a real INotifier
    1public class SlackNotifier : INotifier {
    2 public Task SendAsync(Message m) {
    3 throw new NotImplementedException(
    4 "Slack off in this environment");
    5 }
    6}
    7 
    8public async Task Send(Message m) {
    9 _log.Write(m);
    10 foreach (var x in _n)
    11 await x.SendAsync(m); // Email ran; Slack throws
    12}
    13 
    14// How they call it — same as O
    15await orderNotify.Send(msg); // explodes after Email
    ✔ After — SendAsync always honours the contract
    1public class SlackNotifier : INotifier {
    2 private readonly bool _enabled;
    3 public SlackNotifier(IConfiguration cfg) {
    4 _enabled = cfg.GetValue<bool>("Slack:Enabled");
    5 }
    6 public Task SendAsync(Message m) {
    7 if (!_enabled)
    8 return Task.CompletedTask; // still a successful send
    9 Slack.Post(m.To, m.Text);
    10 return Task.CompletedTask;
    11 }
    12}
    13 
    14// How they call it — same line as O; Slack off is a no-op
    15await orderNotify.Send(msg);

    Takeaway: Callers of INotifier.SendAsync must not explode. Throw is not an implementation.

  • Step 4 — I — Interface segregation
    KindDefinition
    ActualClients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use. Prefer many small interfaces to one fat interface. (Robert C. Martin)
    SimpleDo not put ExportHistory on INotifier. EmailNotifier only sends. History is a different plug.

    Same channels. A report screen needs export/delete of notify.log. Someone dumps those methods onto INotifier. EmailNotifier must compile them — it fakes with throw. A change to ExportHistory recompiles every channel.

    How I solves it: INotifier stays send-only (what OrderNotify needs). History is INotificationHistory. Liskov was “do not surprise SendAsync.” Segregation is “do not even show Export on a sender.”

    ❌ Before — fat INotifier
    1public interface INotifier {
    2 Task SendAsync(Message m);
    3 byte[] ExportHistory();
    4 void DeleteHistory(DateTime before);
    5}
    6 
    7public class EmailNotifier : INotifier {
    8 public Task SendAsync(Message m) {
    9 using var smtp = new SmtpClient("smtp.company.com");
    10 smtp.Send("noreply@co.com", m.To, "Notice", m.Text);
    11 return Task.CompletedTask;
    12 }
    13 public byte[] ExportHistory()
    14 => throw new NotImplementedException();
    15 public void DeleteHistory(DateTime before)
    16 => throw new NotImplementedException();
    17}
    18 
    19// How they call it
    20await orderNotify.Send(msg);
    21emailNotifier.ExportHistory(); // throws — Email is not a report store
    ✔ After — send vs history
    1public interface INotifier {
    2 Task SendAsync(Message m);
    3}
    4 
    5public interface INotificationHistory {
    6 byte[] ExportHistory();
    7 void DeleteHistory(DateTime before);
    8}
    9 
    10public class EmailNotifier : INotifier {
    11 public Task SendAsync(Message m) {
    12 using var smtp = new SmtpClient("smtp.company.com");
    13 smtp.Send("noreply@co.com", m.To, "Notice", m.Text);
    14 return Task.CompletedTask;
    15 }
    16}

    18public class NotificationStore : INotificationHistory {
    19 public byte[] ExportHistory() {
    20 return File.ReadAllBytes("notify.log");
    21 }
    22 public void DeleteHistory(DateTime before) {
    23 /* trim notify.log older than before */
    24 }
    25}

    27// How they call it — two plugs, two callers
    28await orderNotify.Send(msg); // INotifier
    29byte[] csv = store.ExportHistory(); // INotificationHistory

    Takeaway: OrderNotify depends on INotifier only. The report depends on INotificationHistory. EmailNotifier never sees Delete.

  • Step 5 — D — Dependency inversion
    KindDefinition
    ActualHigh-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions. Abstractions should not depend on details; details should depend on abstractions. (Robert C. Martin)
    SimpleEmailNotifier depends on IEmailClient, not new SmtpClient(). DI hands the real mailer or a fake.

    Same EmailNotifier still does new SmtpClient() (from S). That glues the channel to one SMTP class. Tests need a real mail server. Swap to SendGrid → you edit EmailNotifier.

    How D solves it: EmailNotifier (high level) depends on IEmailClient, not SmtpClient. DI hands SmtpEmailClient in production and a fake in tests. INotifier (O) is which channel. IEmailClient (D) is how email actually goes out. new is fine for Message — not for the mailer.

    ❌ Before — glued to SMTP
    1public class EmailNotifier : INotifier {
    2 public Task SendAsync(Message m) {
    3 using var smtp = new SmtpClient("smtp.company.com");
    4 smtp.Send("noreply@co.com", m.To, "Notice", m.Text);
    5 return Task.CompletedTask;
    6 }
    7}
    8 
    9// How they call it — needs a real mail server
    10await new EmailNotifier().SendAsync(msg);
    ✔ After — inject the mailer
    1public interface IEmailClient {
    2 void Send(string from, string to,
    3 string subject, string body);
    4}
    5 
    6public class SmtpEmailClient : IEmailClient {
    7 public void Send(string from, string to,
    8 string subject, string body) {
    9 using var smtp = new SmtpClient("smtp.company.com");
    10 smtp.Send(from, to, subject, body);
    11 }
    12}
    13 
    14public class EmailNotifier : INotifier {
    15 private readonly IEmailClient _email;
    16 public EmailNotifier(IEmailClient email) {
    17 _email = email;
    18 }
    19 public Task SendAsync(Message m) {
    20 _email.Send("noreply@co.com", m.To, "Notice", m.Text);
    21 return Task.CompletedTask;
    22 }
    23}
    24 
    25builder.Services.AddTransient<IEmailClient, SmtpEmailClient>();
    26builder.Services.AddTransient<INotifier, EmailNotifier>();
    27 
    28// How they call it — production vs test
    29await orderNotify.Send(msg); // DI: SmtpEmailClient
    30await new EmailNotifier(fakeEmail).SendAsync(msg); // test: no SMTP

    Takeaway: Channel plug = INotifier. Transport plug = IEmailClient. Do not new SmtpClient inside EmailNotifier.

Quick reference

IdeaRemember
S — Single responsibilityActual: a class should have only one reason to change. Simple: one class, one job. Split the god Notifier: EmailNotifier only emails, SmsNotifier only texts, NotificationLog only logs. No interface yet.
O — Open/ClosedActual: open for extension, closed for modification. Simple: add SlackNotifier (new file); do not reopen EmailNotifier or OrderNotify. How: interface or abstract class (the plug) + polymorphism + DI (IEnumerable<INotifier> + one AddTransient). sealed is not OCP.
L — Liskov substitutionActual: a subtype must replace the parent without breaking the caller. Simple: every INotifier.SendAsync must send or no-op — never throw NotImplemented.
I — Interface segregationActual: do not force clients to depend on methods they do not use. Simple: ExportHistory is not on INotifier. History is INotificationHistory.
D — Dependency inversionActual: depend on abstractions, not details. Simple: inject IEmailClient. Do not new SmtpClient() inside EmailNotifier.

1. S — Single responsibility — full example

Actual: a class should have only one reason to change. Simple: one class, one job. Split the god Notifier: EmailNotifier only emails, SmsNotifier only texts, NotificationLog only logs. No interface yet.

❌ Before
1public class Notifier {
2 public void Notify(string type, Message m) {
3 File.AppendAllText("notify.log", m.Text);
4 if (type == "Email") new SmtpClient().Send(...);
5 else if (type == "Sms") Twilio.Send(...);
6 }
7}
8 
9// How they call it
10new Notifier().Notify("Email", msg);
✔ After
1public class EmailNotifier {
2 public void Send(Message m) {
3 using var smtp = new SmtpClient("smtp.company.com");
4 smtp.Send("noreply@co.com", m.To, "Notice", m.Text);
5 }
6}
7public class SmsNotifier {
8 public void Send(Message m) { Twilio.Send(m.To, m.Text); }
9}
10public class OrderNotify {
11 public void Send(string type, Message m) {
12 if (type == "Email") new EmailNotifier().Send(m);
13 else if (type == "Sms") new SmsNotifier().Send(m);
14 }
15}
16 
17// How they call it — no INotifier yet

Takeaway: S — Single responsibility — explain with a project story, not only a definition.

2. O — Open/Closed — full example

Actual: open for extension, closed for modification. Simple: add SlackNotifier (new file); do not reopen EmailNotifier or OrderNotify. How: interface or abstract class (the plug) + polymorphism + DI (IEnumerable<INotifier> + one AddTransient). sealed is not OCP.

❌ Before
1public class OrderNotify {
2 public void Send(string type, Message m) {
3 if (type == "Email") new EmailNotifier().Send(m);
4 else if (type == "Sms") new SmsNotifier().Send(m);
5 // Slack? edit THIS method again
6 }
7}
8 
9new OrderNotify().Send("Email", msg);
✔ After
1public interface INotifier { Task SendAsync(Message m); }
2public class EmailNotifier : INotifier { /* SendAsync SMTP */ }
3public class SlackNotifier : INotifier { /* NEW FILE */ }
4public class OrderNotify {
5 public OrderNotify(IEnumerable<INotifier> n) { _n = n; }
6 public async Task Send(Message m) {
7 foreach (var x in _n) await x.SendAsync(m);
8 }
9}
10 
11// How they call it — no type string
12await orderNotify.Send(msg);

Takeaway: O — Open/Closed — explain with a project story, not only a definition.

3. L — Liskov substitution — full example

Actual: a subtype must replace the parent without breaking the caller. Simple: every INotifier.SendAsync must send or no-op — never throw NotImplemented.

❌ Before
1public class SlackNotifier : INotifier {
2 public Task SendAsync(Message m) {
3 throw new NotImplementedException("Slack off");
4 }
5}
6 
7await orderNotify.Send(msg); // explodes
✔ After
1public class SlackNotifier : INotifier {
2 public Task SendAsync(Message m) {
3 if (!_enabled) return Task.CompletedTask;
4 Slack.Post(m.To, m.Text);
5 return Task.CompletedTask;
6 }
7}
8 
9await orderNotify.Send(msg); // Email sends, Slack no-ops

Takeaway: L — Liskov substitution — explain with a project story, not only a definition.

4. I — Interface segregation — full example

Actual: do not force clients to depend on methods they do not use. Simple: ExportHistory is not on INotifier. History is INotificationHistory.

Interview — questions & answers

Q: Give actual vs simple definition for each SOLID letter.

A: S actual: one reason to change. Simple: one class, one job. O actual: open for extension, closed for modification. Simple: new Slack class, do not edit OrderNotify. L actual: subtype replaces parent without breaking the caller. Simple: SendAsync must not throw. I actual: do not force unused methods. Simple: history is not on INotifier. D actual: depend on abstractions, not details. Simple: inject IEmailClient, do not new SmtpClient.

Q: Walk SOLID on notification. How did you use it?

A: S: EmailNotifier only emails, SmsNotifier only texts, log is its own class. O: INotifier, Slack was a new file, OrderNotify not edited. L: SendAsync never throws NotImplemented. I: history is INotificationHistory, not on INotifier. D: EmailNotifier gets IEmailClient in the constructor.

Q: Open/Closed — how do you extend without editing? Is that sealed?

A: Two tools: (1) interface or abstract class — INotifier is the plug; SlackNotifier is a new class that fits it. Abstract class if subclasses share code; interface if it is only a capability. (2) DI — OrderNotify takes IEnumerable; AddTransient is the only new line. sealed is different — it blocks subclassing, not OCP.

Q: Liskov vs interface segregation on INotifier?

A: Liskov: every INotifier.SendAsync must succeed like Email — no throw. ISP: do not put ExportHistory on INotifier just because EmailNotifier exists. Split INotificationHistory.

Slide 9 of 21 · C3 — .NET backend
Repository, Unit of Work, Singleton pattern
What this primarily describes: Repository, Unit of Work, Singleton pattern — Design patterns they expect named from YOUR project.

Definition

This slide is three patterns. First is the Repository pattern — a door to one table (IOrderRepository); the service never writes SQL. Then Unit of Work = one SaveChanges for Order + OrderLine. Then Singleton = one instance for the process (cache / settings) — never DbContext, never the repository. They ask all three. Do not mix the names.
  • Repository pattern: Actual: abstraction between business logic and data access. Simple: OrderService talks to IOrderRepository, not DbContext. Hide SQL. Tests mock the interface. Steps below: interface → EF class → inject into the service.
  • Unit of Work pattern: Actual: one business transaction over several repositories. Simple: two repos, one SaveChangesAsync. Complete = SaveChanges succeeds. Repos do not commit.
  • Singleton pattern: Actual: exactly one instance for the process (private ctor or AddSingleton). Simple: cache/settings yes. DbContext / repository / UoW = Scoped, never Singleton.
  • Do not mix them: Interface + DI is wiring (C08). Repository is hide the table. UoW is one commit. Singleton is one object. A repo is not a Singleton.
⛶
Visual guide — Repository and Unit of Work Three patterns: Repository hides SQL. UoW = one SaveChanges. Singleton = cache, never DbContext.

Repository and Unit of Work – Visual Guide

Step-by-step (beginner friendly)

  • Step 1 — Repository pattern, Unit of Work, Singleton — map
    PatternActualSimpleYOUR class
    Repository patternAbstraction between business logic and data access.Door to one table. Service never writes SQL.IOrderRepository / OrderRepository
    Unit of Work patternOne business transaction across several repositories.Order + line → one SaveChanges. Fail → nothing commits.IUnitOfWork wrapping the scoped DbContext
    Singleton patternExactly one instance for the whole process.Cache / settings. Not the database.AddSingleton<IMemoryCache> or private ctor
    LifetimeUse
    AddScopedDbContext, each repository, Unit of Work, OrderService — one set per HTTP request
    AddSingletonMemory cache, app settings — one for the app. Never DbContext.

    Walk them in order: Repository (hide SQL) → Unit of Work (one commit) → Singleton (only if they ask cache / private ctor).

    Takeaway: Three names, three jobs. A repo is not a Singleton. SaveChanges is not a repository method.

  • Step 2 — Repository pattern — what it is
    KindDefinition
    ActualAn abstraction between business logic and data access. The service talks to a contract, not to SQL or EF.
    SimpleA door to one table. OrderService calls IOrderRepository. It never writes SQL and never uses DbContext.

    Blogs often show IProductRepository. Same shape — YOUR class is IOrderRepository.

    BenefitMeansIn this story
    Separation of concernsData access and business rules stay in different classes.EF lives in OrderRepository. Place-order rules live in OrderService.
    TestabilityUnit tests fake the interface.Fake IOrderRepository returns one Order. No SQL Server in the test.
    FlexibilitySwap the data source; the service stays.EF today, Dapper tomorrow — still IOrderRepository.
    ReuseOne repo, many callers.OrderService and a report job both inject the same interface.

    Interface + DI is how you wire it (same idea as INotifier on C08). Repository is what it is for: hide the table.

    Takeaway: Service → IOrderRepository → EF. Not service → DbContext.

  • Step 3 — Repository pattern — define the interface

    List the operations for one entity. No EF types on the interface — that would glue the service to EF.

    ❌ Before — SQL in the service
    1public class OrderService {
    2 public Order Get(int id) {
    3 using var db = new AppDbContext();
    4 return db.Orders.Find(id); // service knows EF
    5 }
    6}
    7 
    8// How they call it
    9new OrderService().Get(42);
    ✔ After — contract only
    1public class Order {
    2 public int Id { get; set; }
    3 public string Customer { get; set; }
    4}
    5 
    6public interface IOrderRepository {
    7 IEnumerable<Order> GetAll();
    8 Order GetById(int id);
    9 void Add(Order order);
    10 void Update(Order order);
    11 void Delete(Order order);
    12}
    13 
    14// How they call it — later, through the service
    15orderService.GetById(42);

    Takeaway: The interface is the plug. OrderService will depend on this, not on AppDbContext.

  • Step 4 — Repository pattern — implement with EF (no SaveChanges)

    The class talks to the database. Inject the scoped DbContext. Track changes only — do not commit inside Add/Update/Delete. Commit belongs to Unit of Work (next step).

    ❌ Before — SaveChanges in every method
    1public class OrderRepository : IOrderRepository {
    2 private readonly AppDbContext _db;
    3 public OrderRepository(AppDbContext db) { _db = db; }
    4 
    5 public IEnumerable<Order> GetAll()
    6 => _db.Orders.ToList();
    7 
    8 public Order GetById(int id)
    9 => _db.Orders.Find(id);
    10 
    11 public void Add(Order order) {
    12 _db.Orders.Add(order);
    13 _db.SaveChanges(); // commits now — UoW is dead
    14 }
    15 public void Update(Order order) {
    16 _db.Orders.Update(order);
    17 _db.SaveChanges();
    18 }
    19 public void Delete(Order order) {
    20 _db.Orders.Remove(order);
    21 _db.SaveChanges();
    22 }
    23}
    ✔ After — track only
    1public class OrderRepository : IOrderRepository {
    2 private readonly AppDbContext _db;
    3 public OrderRepository(AppDbContext db) { _db = db; }
    4 
    5 public IEnumerable<Order> GetAll()
    6 => _db.Orders.ToList();
    7 
    8 public Order GetById(int id)
    9 => _db.Orders.Find(id);
    10 
    11 public void Add(Order order)
    12 => _db.Orders.Add(order); // no SaveChanges
    13 
    14 public void Update(Order order)
    15 => _db.Orders.Update(order);
    16 
    17 public void Delete(Order order)
    18 => _db.Orders.Remove(order);
    19}
    20 
    21builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(...);
    22builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, OrderRepository>();

    Takeaway: Repo = EF for one table. SaveChanges is not a repository method.

  • Step 5 — Repository pattern — use it in the service

    Business logic depends on IOrderRepository. DI hands OrderRepository in production and a fake in tests. Callers never new OrderRepository().

    ❌ Before — new the repo
    1public class OrderService {
    2 public void Create(Order order) {
    3 var repo = new OrderRepository(new AppDbContext());
    4 repo.Add(order); // glued; cannot mock
    5 }
    6}
    7 
    8// How they call it
    9new OrderService().Create(order);
    ✔ After — inject the interface
    1public class OrderService {
    2 private readonly IOrderRepository _orders;
    3 public OrderService(IOrderRepository orders) {
    4 _orders = orders;
    5 }
    6 public IEnumerable<Order> GetAll() => _orders.GetAll();
    7 public Order GetById(int id) => _orders.GetById(id);
    8 public void Create(Order order) => _orders.Add(order);
    9 public void Update(Order order) => _orders.Update(order);
    10 public void Delete(int id) {
    11 var row = _orders.GetById(id);
    12 if (row != null) _orders.Delete(row);
    13 }
    14}
    15 
    16builder.Services.AddScoped<OrderService>();
    17 
    18// How they call it — controller
    19public class OrdersController {
    20 private readonly OrderService _svc;
    21 public OrdersController(OrderService svc) { _svc = svc; }
    22 public IActionResult Get(int id) => Ok(_svc.GetById(id));
    23 public IActionResult Post(Order order) {
    24 _svc.Create(order);
    25 return Created($"/orders/{order.Id}", order);
    26 }
    27}

    Takeaway: Controller → OrderService → IOrderRepository. Tests fake the interface.

  • Step 6 — Unit of Work pattern — one SaveChanges
    KindDefinition
    ActualOne business transaction: several repositories share one context; complete = one commit.
    SimpleOrder + OrderLine → two repos, one SaveChangesAsync. Fail → nothing commits.

    Why it is not Repository: Repository hides SQL for one table. Unit of Work decides when the database commit happens. EF’s DbContext already tracks changes — IUnitOfWork is that commit, so OrderService never takes DbContext.

    If Add on the repo already called SaveChanges, the header is in the database before the line insert runs.

    The concrete class is UnitOfWork (it implements IUnitOfWork). Same scoped AppDbContext as the repositories. It does not run SQL itself — it calls _db.SaveChangesAsync().

    ❌ Before — two commits
    1using var db1 = new AppDbContext();
    2_orders.Add(o); // SaveChanges inside repo
    3using var db2 = new AppDbContext();
    4_lines.Add(line); // second commit — or crash, header already saved
    5 
    6// How they call it
    7new OrderService().Place(order, line); // two transactions
    ✔ After — concrete UnitOfWork + one transaction
    1public interface IUnitOfWork {
    2 Task<int> SaveChangesAsync();
    3}
    4 
    5// CONCRETE CLASS
    6public class UnitOfWork : IUnitOfWork {
    7 private readonly AppDbContext _db;
    8 public IOrderRepository Orders { get; }
    9 public IOrderLineRepository Lines { get; }
    10 
    11 public UnitOfWork(AppDbContext db,
    12 IOrderRepository orders,
    13 IOrderLineRepository lines) {
    14 _db = db;
    15 Orders = orders;
    16 Lines = lines;
    17 }
    18 
    19 public Task<int> SaveChangesAsync() {
    20 return _db.SaveChangesAsync(); // one commit
    21 }
    22}
    23 
    24public class OrderService {
    25 private readonly IUnitOfWork _uow;
    26 public OrderService(IUnitOfWork uow) { _uow = uow; }
    27 public async Task Place(Order o, OrderLine line) {
    28 _uow.Orders.Add(o); // track
    29 _uow.Lines.Add(line); // track
    30 await _uow.SaveChangesAsync(); // ONE commit
    31 }
    32}
    33 
    34builder.Services.AddScoped<AppDbContext>();
    35builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, OrderRepository>();
    36builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderLineRepository, OrderLineRepository>();
    37builder.Services.AddScoped<IUnitOfWork, UnitOfWork>(); // interface → concrete
    38 
    39// How they call it
    40await orderService.Place(order, line);
    41// Complete = SaveChangesAsync returns without exception → 201

    Takeaway: Interface = IUnitOfWork. Concrete = class UnitOfWork. Repos track. UoW commits. Same scoped DbContext.

  • Step 7 — Singleton pattern — one instance, not the database
    KindDefinition
    ActualEnsure a class has only one instance, and provide a global access point (private constructor + static Instance), or register one instance in DI (AddSingleton).
    SimpleOne object for the whole app. Cache and settings yes. DbContext, repository, and Unit of Work no — those are Scoped (one per HTTP request).
    They askSay
    How do you create it if the constructor is private?Only the class can new. A static field builds it once. Callers use AppSettings.Instance — they never new.
    Singleton vs static class?Singleton is still an object (can implement an interface, inject, mock). Static is just a type name — harder to fake in tests.
    Singleton vs Scoped?Singleton = one for the process. Scoped = one per request. DbContext must be Scoped or the change-tracker leaks across users.
    ❌ Before — wrong Singleton
    1builder.Services.AddSingleton<AppDbContext>();
    2builder.Services.AddSingleton<IOrderRepository, OrderRepository>();
    3// tracker leaks; User A sees User B’s tracked rows
    4 
    5public class OrderService {
    6 public void Place(Order o) {
    7 OrderRepository.Instance.Add(o); // not a repo — a global
    8 }
    9}
    10 
    11// How they call it
    12OrderService.Instance.Place(order); // cannot mock; shared across requests
    ✔ After — Singleton only for cache/settings
    1// Classic Singleton — private ctor
    2public class AppSettings {
    3 private static readonly AppSettings _i = new AppSettings();
    4 private AppSettings() { }
    5 public static AppSettings Instance => _i;
    6 public string Region { get; } = "east-us";
    7}
    8 
    9// DI Singleton — same idea, container holds the one instance
    10public interface IPriceCache {
    11 decimal? Get(string sku);
    12 void Set(string sku, decimal price);
    13}
    14public class PriceCache : IPriceCache {

Unit of Work patternActual: one business transaction over several repositories. Simple: two repos, one SaveChangesAsync. Complete = SaveChanges succeeds. Repos do not commit.
