Interview — questions & answers

Q: Walk Repository, Unit of Work, and Singleton on YOUR OrderService.

A: Repository: IOrderRepository hides SQL; OrderService never uses DbContext. Unit of Work: Add order and line then one SaveChangesAsync — fail and nothing commits. Singleton: IPriceCache is AddSingleton; DbContext and the repos stay Scoped. A repository is not a Singleton.

Q: How do you implement it in C#?

A: Three steps: define IOrderRepository (GetAll, GetById, Add, Update, Delete). Implement it with the scoped DbContext. Inject IOrderRepository into OrderService. Register AddScoped.

Q: What is Unit of Work? Three repositories insert together?

A: UoW is one business transaction. Repos only track changes. All three share the scoped DbContext. I call SaveChanges once. Failure → no commit. Do not SaveChanges inside the repo Add method.

Q: How do you know the operation completed?

A: SaveChangesAsync returns without exception; I return 201. The request-scoped context disposes at the end of the request.

Q: Private constructor — how do you create the object?

A: Only the class can construct. Factory method or static Instance, or DI. Callers never new. Not for DbContext.

Q: Why design patterns? Is interface + DI already Repository?

A: Interface + DI is how you wire it (same as INotifier). Repository is what the class is for: one table, hide SQL. UoW is one SaveChanges. Not because a blog said so.

LINQ: IQueryable vs IEnumerable, left join
What this primarily describes: LINQ: IQueryable vs IEnumerable, left join — Deferred execution and the left outer join they keep asking.

Definition

IQueryable = an expression EF can still turn into SQL (server). IEnumerable = data already in memory (C#). They also ask a left outer join in LINQ — keep the left row even if the right side is missing.
  • What it is: IQueryable is deferred SQL. IEnumerable is in-memory LINQ. ToList() runs SQL now. Left join = keep customers with no orders (GroupJoin + DefaultIfEmpty / SQL LEFT JOIN).
  • How you use it: Filter on IQueryable. ToListAsync in the repository while the context is open. Then Count and foreach the same list. Left join: join … into g from x in g.DefaultIfEmpty().
  • Purpose / impact: Purpose: let SQL filter 1 million rows; do not pull them into C# first. Impact: loop IQueryable after Dispose → crash. Count() then foreach the same IQueryable → two SQL trips. Where on IEnumerable after a bad ToList → table scan in memory.
  • ToList(): Run SQL now, while the context is open. Then you can count and loop the same list. Take(3) becomes TOP 3.
⛶
Visual guide — IQueryable vs IEnumerable IQueryable = SQL still runs on the server. IEnumerable = data is already in memory.

Interview — questions & answers

Q: IQueryable vs IEnumerable?

A: IQueryable can become SQL and is deferred. IEnumerable runs in memory. After ToList you have IEnumerable. Do not return IQueryable from a disposed context.

Q: How do you perform a left outer join in LINQ?

A: from a in db.A join b in db.B on a.Id equals b.AId into g from b in g.DefaultIfEmpty() select new { a, b }.

Q: Select top 3 with EF?

A: OrderByDescending(...).Take(3).ToListAsync() — Take becomes TOP 3.

EF, Fluent API, stored procedures
What this primarily describes: EF, Fluent API, stored procedures — ORM types, Code First vs DB First, run SP from EF, many-to-many.

Definition

EF (Entity Framework) is an ORM — objects map to tables. Fluent API configures keys, indexes, and relationships in OnModelCreating. A heavy stored procedure is still called as an SP — do not hide it. Be honest: Code First (migrations) vs DB First (scaffold).
  • What it is: ORM = Object-Relational Mapper. They expect EF Core. Dapper is a thin mapper. ADO.NET is not an ORM. Fluent API = configuration in code. SP = stored procedure you still EXEC.
  • How you use it: Relationships/indexes in OnModelCreating. Query SP: FromSqlRaw with parameters. Command SP: ExecuteSql. Many-to-many: join entity if you need extra columns.
  • Purpose / impact: Purpose: CRUD in C#; keep complex reports in SQL. Impact: concatenate SQL into FromSql → injection. Only attributes → missing indexes. Pretend EF wrote every SP → they hand you a 100-line proc and you freeze.
  • Code First vs DB First: Code First = C# owns the tables (migrations). DB First = database already exists, we scaffold. Say which you used. Neither is “wrong.”
⛶
Visual guide — EF Fluent API stored procedures Fluent API configures tables in code. For a heavy stored procedure, call it — do not hide it.

Interview — questions & answers

Q: Can we run a stored procedure from Entity Framework?

A: Yes. FromSqlRaw for queries mapped to a type; ExecuteSql for commands. Parameters — never concatenate SQL.

Q: What is Fluent API?

A: Configuration in OnModelCreating instead of (or plus) attributes. We used it for composite keys, indexes, and delete behavior.

Q: Many-to-many in EF?

A: Join table OrderTag(OrderId, TagId). Skip navigation in EF Core 5+ or an explicit join entity if we need payload columns.

Middleware, filters, async/await
What this primarily describes: Middleware, filters, async/await — Pipeline order, custom middleware on some actions, Task vs Thread.

Definition

Middleware is the ASP.NET pipeline: every HTTP request goes in, then out in reverse (an onion). async/await frees the thread while waiting on SQL — the method still waits at await. Per-action rules belong on a filter or [Authorize], not on global Use().
  • What it is: Middleware = app.Use around the whole request (JWT, logging, CORS). Filter = MVC, can see the action. async = a Task that completes later. Thread = OS worker; Task ≠ extra thread for I/O.
  • How you use it: JWT auth middleware is global. Correlation id is global. “Only some actions” = action filter or attribute. await next() then code on the way out. Dependent work: await A then await B. Independent: Task.WhenAll.
  • Purpose / impact: Purpose: one place for cross-cutting HTTP (auth, timing). Await so the thread is not blocked on SQL. Impact: .Result → deadlock. Global Use() on health checks → health needs a JWT. “After response, middleware runs again” is the outbound pass, not a second request.
  • async: Await f2() in f1 DOES wait for f2 before the next line. The thread pool thread is released during I/O. That is not Thread.Sleep. Task is a unit of work / promise.
⛶

Interview — questions & answers

Q: After returning the response, does middleware execute again?

A: Code after await next() runs on the way out — logging, timing. That is not a second HTTP request.

Q: Custom middleware for some actions only?

A: Prefer an action filter or [Authorize] on those actions. Or branch with endpoint.Metadata. Global Use() hits every request including health checks.

Q: f1 async calls f2 async — does the thread wait?

A: The method f1 waits at await f2() for f2 to finish before the next line. The thread pool thread is released during the I/O wait. That is not Thread.Sleep.

Q: Task vs Thread?

A: Thread is an OS thread. Task is a unit of work / promise. I/O APIs use Tasks without occupying a thread the whole time. CPU work may run on a pool thread.

OOP: abstract, virtual, base, sealed
What this primarily describes: OOP: abstract, virtual, base, sealed — Scenario OOP — not definitions only.

Definition

OOP keywords they give as a scenario, not a glossary. abstract = child MUST write the method (no body in the parent — GetPet, Log). virtual = child MAY replace a default (Play). sealed = nobody inherits further. Two interfaces with the same method → implement at least one explicitly.
  • What it is: abstract GetPet() = child MUST write it. virtual Play() = child MAY keep the default. abstract Log on BaseLogger. sealed = nobody inherits further (DogPerson as a leaf). Two interfaces with the same method → implement at least one explicitly.
  • How you use it: Abstract when every child must implement (GetPet, Log). Virtual when the base default is fine (Play). base() for shared fields. Two interfaces: void IFoo.Do() vs void IBar.Do().
  • Purpose / impact: Purpose: force the rule you need, allow the override you do not. Impact: empty override that throws → Liskov break. Forget explicit interface → the wrong Do() runs. Sealed on a type you later need to extend → stuck.
  • sealed / private ctor: Sealed = no subclass (DogPerson as a leaf). Private constructor = Singleton or factory — callers never new. Not the same as OCP (OCP uses a new class, not sealed).

Q: Abstract vs virtual methods?

A: Abstract GetPet forces DogPerson and CatLover to write it. Virtual Play has a default they can keep. Abstract Log on BaseLogger. Interface is a contract with no base behavior (until default interface methods).

Q: Use of the base keyword?

A: Call the parent constructor or a parent method we are extending. this is the current object.

A: Implement at least one explicitly: void ILogger.Log(...) so the caller casts to the interface they mean.

SQL isolation and indexes
What this primarily describes: SQL isolation and indexes — Isolation level choice + clustered vs nonclustered.

Definition

Isolation = how much one transaction may see of another’s uncommitted work. Index = a lookup structure so SQL does not scan the whole table. They ask which isolation you used, and clustered vs nonclustered — clustered is not “always better.”
  • What it is: Read Committed (SQL Server default) = you do not see someone else’s uncommitted write. Snapshot/RCSI = readers use a row version, less blocking. Clustered = the table’s order (one per table). Nonclustered = extra lookup tree.
  • How you use it: Stay on Read Committed unless you have a reason. Hot report vs OLTP → consider RCSI, not NOLOCK. One clustered (usually PK). Nonclustered on the columns the SP actually filters — from the actual plan.
  • Purpose / impact: Purpose: correct reads + fast lookups. Impact: NOLOCK → dirty reads (wrong money). GUID clustered PK → fragmentation. Too many nonclustered → slow inserts. Wide clustered key → every other index gets heavier.
  • Clustered vs nonclustered: Only one clustered. The table itself is stored in that order. Nonclustered helps WHERE/JOIN. Not a substitute for a surrogate key on a huge varchar.
⛶

How you use itStay on Read Committed unless you have a reason. Hot report vs OLTP → consider RCSI, not NOLOCK. One clustered (usually PK). Nonclustered on the columns the SP actually filters — from the actual plan.
Purpose / impactPurpose: correct reads + fast lookups. Impact: NOLOCK → dirty reads (wrong money). GUID clustered PK → fragmentation. Too many nonclustered → slow inserts. Wide clustered key → every other index gets heavier.
Clustered vs nonclusteredOnly one clustered. The table itself is stored in that order. Nonclustered helps WHERE/JOIN. Not a substitute for a surrogate key on a huge varchar.

Read Committed (SQL Server default) = you do not see someone else’s uncommitted write. Snapshot/RCSI = readers use a row version, less blocking. Clustered = the table’s order (one per table). Nonclustered = extra lookup tree.

Interview — questions & answers

Q: What is isolation? Which did you use?

A: Isolation is how one transaction sees others. We used the default Read Committed. Snapshot if they need readers without blocking.

Q: Clustered vs nonclustered? Disadvantage of clustered?

A: Only one clustered. A wide clustered key bloats every nonclustered index. Random GUID as clustered PK causes fragmentation.

Q: Index on varchar?

A: Yes if the column is selective and used in WHERE/JOIN. Prefix length and included columns matter. Not a substitute for a surrogate key.

SP performance, deadlock, temp tables
What this primarily describes: SP performance, deadlock, temp tables — They will hand you a long SP or ask how you tune without prod access.

Definition

A slow stored procedure is usually a scan, a bad join, or a deadlock. Read the actual plan before rewriting. They may hand you a long SP, or ask how you tune with no prod access.
  • What it is: Tune = reproduce → actual plan → stats → parameter sniffing → rewrite row-by-row → one index → measure. Temp table (#) = staged set with statistics. Table variable = tiny, weak stats. CTE = not stored, not a magic speed-up. Deadlock = two sessions wait on each other; SQL kills one (1205).
  • How you use it: Staging copy + ticket parameters. Actual plan, STATISTICS IO. Big intermediate set → #temp + index it. Same lock order in both procs. CATCH 1205 and retry. No prod: logs, Event Viewer, masked restore — never guess.
  • Purpose / impact: Purpose: make the SP use seeks; not lose a transaction silently. Impact: guess 12 indexes → still slow. Table variable for a million rows → bad plan. Ignore deadlock graph → it keeps happening. “I need prod” with no RCA path → they fail the legacy round.
  • No prod access: Logs they can export, IIS status, request id, staging SP with the same parameters. Several sessions asked this.

Interview — questions & answers

Q: How do you handle performance in SQL / optimize an SP?

A: Actual plan, SET STATISTICS IO, find the worst operator, index or rewrite, watch parameter sniffing (OPTIMIZE FOR / local variables / recompile as last resort).

Q: Why temp tables in SQL?

A: Stage a large set once, index it, reuse. Better stats than a table variable for big data.

Q: Deadlock — prevent and after it happens?

A: Same lock order, less work in the transaction, snapshot. After: read the deadlock graph, retry the victim, fix the query/index.

Q: Second max / rows in A not in B?

A: Second max: OFFSET/ROW_NUMBER or MAX where < max. A not in B: NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN ... WHERE b.Key IS NULL.

SQL execution plans
What this primarily describes: SQL execution plans — Capture the actual plan, read it, name the operator, fix, retest.

Definition

An execution plan is how SQL Server fetched the rows. We use database MyDB (Customer, Product, Orders as a heap, OrderLine). Heap = no clustered index — that is why Step 0 is a Table Scan. Tune from the actual plan (Ctrl+M): one index or one rewrite, then retest.
  • What it is: Estimated (Ctrl+L) = guess, query does not run. Actual (Ctrl+M) = query runs; actual rows and warnings. Cost % is still an estimate.
  • How you use it: Scripts: 00_create_mydb.sql (you, as user1) → 01_mydb_schema_seed.sql → 02_mydb_tune_steps.sql. Highlight one step, Ctrl+M, F5.
  • Purpose / impact: Purpose: see Table Scan become Seek. Impact: twelve indexes with no picture; YEAR(CreatedUtc); Status = 1 on a varchar column.
  • Why Orders is a heap: Seed created Orders with columns only — no clustered PK. Object Explorer: Indexes folder empty. sys.indexes = HEAP, 50,000 rows. Left that way so the first actual plan is Table Scan.
  • Hover the operator: Object = what was read (heap = table name, no index). Predicate = residual WHERE — does not skip pages on a scan. Output List = columns out, not row count. Rows Read vs Actual Rows = touched vs kept.
  • MyDB story: Heap Table Scan 50k read. CX on OrderId still 50k. NCI key = WHERE, INCLUDE = SELECT extras → Seek 25 read / 25 out.
  • Key vs INCLUDE: Key columns go in the WHERE — SQL uses them to find matching rows (index at the back of a book). INCLUDE columns go in the SELECT — stored with the index so SQL does not go back to the main table.
⛶
Visual guide — How to turn a Table Scan into an Index Seek Find the WHERE key, left to right, equality then range. No YEAR on the column. OR may need UNION ALL. Seek Predicates = the jump. INCLUDE for SELECT so you skip Key Lookup. Measure with the actual plan.

Step-by-step (beginner friendly)

  • Step 1 — What an execution plan is, how you capture it, why it matters

    Open visual guide How to turn a Table Scan into an Index Seek first — flowchart, then our MyDB shots.

    Say this
    WhatThe optimizer’s picture of how it will fetch rows: which index, scan or seek, join type. Actual plan includes runtime rows. Estimated does not run the query.
    How you use itSSMS: Query → Include Actual Execution Plan (Ctrl+M) → Execute. Open the Execution Plan tab. Hover the operator or F4 Properties. Read Object, Predicate, Output List, then the row counts — not cost % alone. Start at SELECT (left), then the 100% operator.
    PurposeName the operator they will point at. One change, then capture the plan again.
    ImpactTune from Messages or from an estimated plan → you miss spills and actual rows. Add 12 indexes with no picture → still a scan.
    WithoutWith
    Messages: (1 row affected)Execution Plan tab: Table Scan on MyDB.dbo.Orders
    OperatorHow to think about itIn our lab
    Table ScanThe table has no clustered index — we call that a heap. SQL has no ordered book, so it reads every page, then checks your WHERE.Step 0, before CX_Orders. Object is just dbo.Orders — no index name.
    Clustered Index ScanNow the table has a clustered index, but your WHERE is not that key. So SQL still walks along the clustered pages. Having an index is not the same as using it for this filter.We clustered on OrderId, but we filtered CustomerId and Status. Object = CX_Orders. Still 50,000 rows read.
    Index Scan (nonclustered)SQL walks a smaller index (not the whole table row), but still start-to-end, then filters. Like flipping every tab in a thinner notebook.The OR query: it scanned IX_Orders_Status_Created and read 50,000 to keep 5,025.
    Clustered Index SeekSQL jumps using the clustered key — here that key is OrderId. “Give me this order number.”Key Lookup does this: it already has OrderId from the NCI, then Seeks CX_Orders.
    Index Seek (nonclustered)SQL jumps using the nonclustered key. Hover Seek Predicates — that is the part of the WHERE that matched the index, like the word in the back-of-the-book index.(CustomerId, Status) → jump to customer 42 / Closed. (Status, CreatedUtc) → jump to Hold, or Open + this year.
    Key LookupSeek found the row in the small index, but SELECT asked for a column that is not sitting in that leaf. So SQL goes back to the clustered table with OrderId. Extra trip. Not always bad — count how many trips.INCLUDE had only Total, SELECT still wanted CreatedUtc. Nested Loops, lookup ~96%.

    Scan vs Seek — say it like this:
    Scan = start at one end and walk, then maybe keep some rows.
    Seek = jump straight to the key.
    If the name says Index Scan or Index Seek, hover Object (which index?) and then Seek Predicates vs Predicate (jump vs leftover filter).

    How do I turn a Scan into a Seek?Do this
    1. Match the WHERE to a keyPut the filter columns in the index key, left to right. CustomerId then Status — not OrderId if you filter CustomerId.
    2. Leave the column bareNo YEAR(CreatedUtc). Use a range: CreatedUtc >= @from AND CreatedUtc < @to.
    3. Matching typesStatus = 'Open', not Status = 1.
    4. One predicate per SeekOR on two columns often scans. UNION ALL + an index for each WHERE can Seek both sides.
    5. Then create the indexRewrite first if needed, then CREATE INDEX. A Seekable query with no index still scans.
    How many indexes?Why
    Clustered: 0 or 1The clustered index is the table — rows live in that key order, like one filing cabinet. You cannot store the same row in two physical orders, so a second clustered index is not allowed. Zero clustered = heap (unordered pages).
    Nonclustered: manyEach NCI is an extra sorted copy of some columns (key + INCLUDE + the clustered pointer). SQL Server allows up to 999 per table. You would never want that many — every INSERT/UPDATE must maintain each NCI. Our lab: two is plenty (CustomerId, Status and Status, CreatedUtc).

    Tree or heap? A heap is not a tree — just a pile of pages. Clustered and nonclustered indexes are B-trees (balanced trees: many keys per node, short height, so a jump is a few page reads). They are not binary trees (a binary tree has only two children per node). Say “B-tree,” not “binary tree.” Seek = walk a few B-tree levels to the key. Scan = walk the leaf left to right.

    Takeaway: One clustered (or a heap). Many NCI, keep them few. Scan → Seek: WHERE matches the key, no function on the column, then build that index. Indexes are B-trees, not binary trees.

  • Step 2 — Create MyDB, then seed (you create the database)

    This Cursor Windows login is not dbcreator. Create the database in SSMS as user1 (or sysadmin), then run the seed.

    -- SSMS as user1, master: CREATE DATABASE [MyDB]; -- file: ClientInterview/sql/00_create_mydb.sql -- then F5: -- ClientInterview/sql/01_mydb_schema_seed.sql
    TableRowsIndex at seed
    Customer~2,000Clustered PK
    Product~200Clustered PK
    Orders~50,000HEAP — no clustered index
    OrderLine~150,000Clustered PK (OrderId, LineNumber)

    Joins: Orders.CustomerId → Customer. OrderLine.OrderId → Orders (logical; FK added after clustered). OrderLine.ProductId → Product.

    Takeaway: You create MyDB. Seed leaves Orders as a heap on purpose.

  • Step 3 — Why Orders is a HEAP

    Open visual guide MyDB — why Orders is a HEAP (your SSMS shot).

    QuestionSay this
    What is a heap?A table with no clustered index. Pages are not ordered by a key.
    How did we get one?CREATE TABLE dbo.Orders listed columns only — no PRIMARY KEY CLUSTERED, no CREATE CLUSTERED INDEX.
    How do you prove it?Object Explorer: Customer / Product / OrderLine show PK_… (Clustered). Orders → Indexes folder is empty. Query: type_desc = HEAP, 50,000 rows.
    Why leave it a heap?On purpose. Step 0 needs a before picture: a filter on CustomerId / Status that still Table Scans the whole table. If we clustered on OrderId from day one, you would skip the heap vs clustered distinction they often ask.

    Heap is not “broken.” It is the default when you do not pick a clustered key. Lookups without a useful nonclustered index walk every page.

    Takeaway: No clustered index = heap. We left Orders that way so the first actual plan is Table Scan.

  • Step 4 — same WHERE, Table Scan (heap)

    Open visual guide Step 0 — Table Scan on the heap. File: 02_mydb_tune_steps.sql. Highlight only this SELECT. Ctrl+M, then Execute. Hover the Table Scan (or F4 Properties). Do not run CX_Orders yet.

    SELECT o.OrderId, o.CustomerId, o.Status, o.Total, o.CreatedUtc FROM dbo.Orders AS o WHERE o.CustomerId = 42 AND o.Status = 'Open';
    Tooltip fieldYour Step 0 valueWhat it indicates
    Object[MyDB].[dbo].[Orders] [o]What was read. Heap = table name only, no index name. After a clustered/NCI you will see CX_Orders or IX_Orders_Customer_Status here.
    PredicateCustomerId = … AND Status = … (often with CONVERT_IMPLICIT)The WHERE applied as a residual filter while/after the scan. It does not mean SQL skipped pages. Convert on the column can block a later Seek — that is Step 4.
    Output ListOrderId, CustomerId, Status, Total, CreatedUtcColumns this operator hands to the next operator (your SELECT list). Not “how many rows.” Wide list / SELECT * later → Key Lookup (Step 2).
    Row number (hover / F4)Your shotImportant?
    Actual Number of Rows Read50,000Yes — I/O work. Rows touched in the object before the residual kept/dropped them. Whole heap.
    Actual Number of Rows (for all executions)0Yes — pair it with rows read. Rows that survived the Predicate and went left to SELECT. 0 in Results ≠ cheap.
    Estimated Number of Rows~8Optimizer’s guess of rows after the filter. Compare to actual 0. Off by 10× on a real app → stats / sniffing. Not the main Step 0 story.

    50,000 is not the only number. The interview line is the pair: read 50,000, returned 0. The filter ran, but only after a full heap scan. Object says heap. Predicate says which filter. Output List says which columns came out.

    Takeaway: Read vs returned. Object = what. Predicate = residual WHERE. Output List = columns, not rows. “50k read / 0 out” proves the WHERE did not skip I/O.

  • Step 5 — Fix 0 — CREATE clustered CX_Orders (Sort + insert)

    Open visual guide Fix 0 — CREATE clustered CX_Orders. Highlight only the CREATE UNIQUE CLUSTERED INDEX (the IF NOT EXISTS batch). Ctrl+M, Execute. Two plans appear — read Query 2.

    IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM sys.indexes WHERE name = N'CX_Orders' AND object_id = OBJECT_ID(N'dbo.Orders')) CREATE UNIQUE CLUSTERED INDEX CX_Orders ON dbo.Orders (OrderId);
    PlanWhat it isIgnore / keep
    Query 1 — COND WITH QUERYIF NOT EXISTS looking up sys.indexesIgnore (0% of the batch). Not your Orders tune.
    Query 2 — Table Scan → Sort → Index InsertBuild the clustered B-tree on OrderIdThis is the create. Table Scan still says heap during the build.
    Query 2 operatorYour shotWhat it indicates
    Table Scan [Orders]50,000 of 50,000Source is still a heap while SQL copies every row.
    Sort~65% cost, 50,000 rowsClustered pages must be in OrderId order. Sort is why create-index can be expensive.
    Index Insert CX_Orders~30%Writes the sorted rows into the clustered index. After this, Object Explorer shows CX_Orders (Clustered). Not a heap anymore.

    Takeaway: Creating clustered = read heap, Sort by the key, insert. The SELECT has not been tuned yet.

    Object[MyDB].[dbo].[Orders].[CX_Orders] [o]Now an index name. Heap is gone. Still not a Seek on CustomerId.
    OperatorClustered Index ScanWalks the clustered index (key = OrderId). Scan ≠ Seek.
    PredicateCustomerId and Status residual (+ convert)Filter still applied while scanning. Clustered key does not match this WHERE.
    Output ListOrderId, CustomerId, Status, Total, CreatedUtcSame SELECT columns handed left. Not the row count.
    Row numberYour shotImportant?
    Actual Number of Rows Read50,000Yes. Still touched every row. Clustered did not skip I/O for this filter.

    Table Scan → Clustered Index Scan is not the win. Same 50,000 rows read. Interview: “Clustered on OrderId. My filter is CustomerId and Status. Residual predicate. I still need a nonclustered on the WHERE.”

    Takeaway: Object = CX_Orders. Scan, not Seek. 50k read / 25 out. Next index must be (CustomerId, Status).

  • Step 7 — NCI: key columns vs INCLUDE

    Open visual guide Step 1 — NCI key columns vs INCLUDE. Highlight only the CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX. Ctrl+M. Object Explorer: CX_Orders (Clustered) plus IX_Orders_Customer_Status (Nonclustered).

    CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_Customer_Status ON dbo.Orders (CustomerId, Status) -- KEY: WHERE — find matching rows INCLUDE (Total, CreatedUtc); -- INCLUDE: SELECT — return without going back to the table
    Key columns (CustomerId, Status)INCLUDE (Total, CreatedUtc)
    PurposeThese are the columns used in the WHERE clause.
    SQL uses them to find the matching rows.
    Think of them like the index at the back of a book — SQL uses them to quickly locate the required data.    		These columns are used in the SELECT (returning data), not in the WHERE (searching).
    They are stored along with the index so SQL can return the required values without going back to the main table.
    Use forWHERE CustomerId = 42 AND Status = 'Closed'. First filter first: CustomerId, then Status.Because the SELECT lists Total and CreatedUtc. A WHERE on Total would not use INCLUDE to Seek.
    SizeCopied at every level of the index. Keep this list short.Only at the bottom. Cheaper than putting Total in the key if you only display it.
    Also at the bottomOrderId is copied in automatically (clustered key). You do not add it to INCLUDE.
    CREATE plan (Query 2)What it indicates
    Clustered Index Scan CX_Orders — 50,000Read the table to build the new index.
    Sort ~65%NCI must be ordered by (CustomerId, Status) — not by OrderId.
    Index Insert IX_Orders_Customer_StatusWrite each leaf row. Writes get a bit slower — that is the cost of the extra index.
    In the NCI leaf (bottom of the index)Example for one matching order
    Key columnsCustomerId = 42, Status = 'Closed' — SQL used these to find this leaf
    INCLUDE columnsTotal, CreatedUtc — already here, so SELECT can return them
    Clustered key (automatic)OrderId — a pointer to the full row in CX_Orders

    When is OrderId used? Only if the SELECT needs a column that is not in this leaf — not in the key, not in INCLUDE, and not OrderId itself. Example: ModifiedDate. That column still lives in the clustered index (the clustered index is the table — every column is there). SQL takes OrderId from the NCI leaf and Seeks CX_Orders. That extra trip is a Key Lookup.

    Our covering SELECT lists OrderId, CustomerId, Status, Total, CreatedUtc — all already in the leaf — so SQL Seeks and stops. No Key Lookup.

    Takeaway: Leaf stores key + INCLUDE + OrderId. Seek uses CustomerId/Status. Lookup uses OrderId only when SELECT asks for a column missing from this index.

    Open visual guide Compare — heap vs clustered scan vs covering Seek. Same SELECT: CustomerId = 42 AND Status = 'Closed'. Hover each 100% operator.

    Heap (before CX)After CX_OrdersAfter NCI + INCLUDE
    OperatorTable ScanClustered Index ScanIndex Seek (NonClustered)
    Objectdbo.Orders (no index name)CX_OrdersIX_Orders_Customer_Status
    Rows Read50,00050,00025
    Actual Rows252525
    Filter fieldPredicate (residual)Predicate (residual)Seek Predicates on CustomerId, Status
    Output List5 SELECT columnssame 5same 5 — from the NCI leaf (INCLUDE + clustered locator). No Key Lookup

    What the comparison proves: Clustered on OrderId did not change rows read (50k / 50k) or cost. The NCI on the WHERE did: rows read dropped to 25, matching actual rows. Predicate vs Seek Predicate: residual = scan then filter; Seek Predicate = navigate the B-tree. INCLUDE is why Output List is complete without a lookup.

    Cost % is still an estimate. The number to quote is 50,000 rows read → 25 rows read.

    Takeaway: Heap scan ≈ clustered scan for this filter. Covering Seek: 25 read / 25 out. Key found the rows; INCLUDE avoided Key Lookup.

  • Step 9 — INCLUDE only Total: Key Lookup + Nested Loops

    Open visual guide Step 2 — INCLUDE only Total → Key Lookup + Nested Loops. Same SELECT as before. Index is now (CustomerId, Status) INCLUDE (Total) only — CreatedUtc is missing from the leaf.

    -- NCI key still finds the rows. INCLUDE has Total only. SELECT o.OrderId, o.CustomerId, o.Status, o.Total, o.CreatedUtc FROM dbo.Orders AS o WHERE o.CustomerId = 42 AND o.Status = 'Closed';
    Operator (hover)PhysicalLogicalWhat it means
    The join in the middleNested LoopsInner JoinTwo names on the same box.
    Physical (Nested Loops) is the method: take one row from the Seek, then look up that OrderId in the clustered index, then the next row, then the next — 25 times, one by one.
    Logical (Inner Join) is the result: keep each pair — Seek columns plus CreatedUtc.
    You did not write a JOIN. SQL added this join only to fetch the missing column.
    Index Seek IX_Orders_Customer_StatusIndex SeekIndex SeekWHERE on the key. Output List: OrderId, CustomerId, Status, Total. No CreatedUtc.
    Key Lookup CX_Orders (~96%)Key LookupKey LookupUses OrderId from the leaf. Output List: CreatedUtc only. Clustered is the table — that column lives there.
    Nested Loops fieldYour shotWhy it matters
    Outer ReferencesOrderIdValue passed from Seek (outer) into Key Lookup (inner) — the pointer we talked about.
    Actual Number of Rows2525 Seeks → about 25 Key Lookups (one per matching order).
    Output Listall 5 SELECT columnsAfter the join, Seek columns + CreatedUtc from the lookup.

    Physical vs logical — say it like this: Physical is the method (how the work is done). Logical is the result (what the operator means). Nested Loops = “one by one.” Inner Join = “keep the matching pair.” You wrote only a SELECT. SQL built this join because CreatedUtc was not in the nonclustered leaf.

    Fix: put CreatedUtc back in INCLUDE (or drop it from the SELECT). Then the leaf is covering again — Seek only, no Nested Loops, no Key Lookup.

    Takeaway: INCLUDE only Total → Seek finds 25 rows, Nested Loops Inner Join looks up CreatedUtc by OrderId. That extra trip is Key Lookup (~96%).

  • Step 10 — Key = CustomerId only — how WHERE Status still works

    Open visual guide Key = CustomerId only — WHERE Status is residual. Index is now (CustomerId) INCLUDE (Total). No key and no INCLUDE for Status or CreatedUtc. Same WHERE: CustomerId = 42 AND Status = 'Closed'.

    WHERE pieceIn the index?Where it runs
    CustomerId = 42KeySeek Predicates on the Index Seek — SQL jumps to customer 42.
    Status = 'Closed'No (not key, not INCLUDE)Predicate on the Key Lookup — after SQL already opened the clustered row by OrderId.
    HoverYour shotSay this
    Index Seek25 of 25. Seek Predicates: CustomerId = 42 only. Output: OrderId, CustomerId, TotalThe key has only CustomerId. SQL jumps to customer 42 and takes all 25 of that customer’s orders — Closed, Open, everything.
    Key LookupRows read 25, actual 19. Predicate: Status = 'Closed'. Output: Status, CreatedUtcFor each of those 25, open the clustered row by OrderId. Then apply Status. 6 not Closed are dropped. 19 Closed remain. Status and CreatedUtc come from the table.
    Nested Loops19 of 25 (76%)Same 25 lookups. Only 19 pairs survive Inner Join after the residual.

    Two questions. First: “Where is customer 42?” — the Seek (25 rows). Second: “Is this order Closed, and what is CreatedUtc?” — SQL must open the full row. That is why Status is a Predicate on the Key Lookup, not a Seek Predicate.

    Who takes the time / cost?Your shotWhy
    Key Lookup~96% — the expensive one25 random trips into CX_Orders (one per Seek row). Opening the clustered page is much heavier than walking the small NCI.
    Index SeekCheap (small leftover %)Narrow index, 25 rows, one jump on CustomerId.
    Nested Loops0% on the icon — it is the boss, not the workerIt only says “do the lookup 25 times.” The cost sits on Key Lookup.
    How to improveWhat you changeWhat will happen
    1. Put Status in the key(CustomerId, Status) INCLUDE (Total)Seek Predicates include Closed. Seek = 19, not 25. Key Lookup runs 19 times, not 25. The 6 Open/Hold rows are never looked up. Status comes from the NCI. You still look up for CreatedUtc — Key Lookup stays, but cheaper.
    2. Also INCLUDE the missing SELECT(CustomerId, Status) INCLUDE (Total, CreatedUtc)The leaf has everything. Seek only — Nested Loops and Key Lookup go away. Like slide-16-06: 19 read / 19 out, tiny cost.

    Do not “fix” this with NOLOCK or twelve extra indexes. One index from the WHERE, then INCLUDE from the SELECT.

    Always avoid Key Lookup?No — look at how many times it runs
    Cover (INCLUDE) whenThe query is hot and Key Lookup executions are many (here: 25, ~96%). Same columns every time.
    A lookup is OK whenOnly a few rows (1–10 lookups), or the extra column is rare / wide. A fat INCLUDE on every write can cost more than a cheap lookup.
    Interview lineI do not INCLUDE every column. I hover Key Lookup: Number of Executions. Many executions on a frequent query → cover. Two lookups on a rare report → leave it.

    Takeaway: Key Lookup ~96% is the wait here. Not every lookup is bad. Many executions + hot query → INCLUDE. Few executions → covering can be worse.

    Open visual guide Step 3 — YEAR() is not Seekable. Hover in this order (or F4). Read right to left: data starts on the right.

    Hover thisLook atSay this
    1. Green missing-index lineImpact %, the CREATE INDEX textA hint, not a command. It wants (Status) INCLUDE (CustomerId, Total, CreatedUtc). It does not fix YEAR(CreatedUtc), and it does not touch the 49% OrderLine scan.
    2. SELECT (left)Warnings (yellow triangle)Start here. Missing index lives on this node too.
    3. OrderLine Clustered Index Scan (49%)Object = PK_OrderLine. Rows = 150,000Biggest cost. COUNT(*) of lines needs every line. Clustered key is (OrderId, LineNumber) — no WHERE on OrderLine, so a scan of the lines table.
    4. Stream AggregateOutput: count per OrderIdTurns 150,000 lines into ~50,000 order counts. That is the COUNT_BIG(*) + GROUP BY.
    5. Orders Clustered Index Scan (19%)Object = CX_Orders. Predicate. Rows ~3,131 of 3,889Scan, not Seek. Hover Predicate: Status = 'Open' and YEAR(CreatedUtc) = …. Function on the column = residual. SQL cannot Seek a date range.
    6. Merge Join (Orders + lines)Physical = Merge Join. Logical = Inner JoinMethod: both sides already in OrderId order, walk together. Result: keep matching orders. Not Nested Loops — both inputs are big and sorted.
    7. Sort (7%)Order ByRe-sort for the next Merge Join (now on CustomerId).
    8. Customer Clustered Index Scan (1%)Object = PK_Customer. 2,000 rowsSmall table. Scan of the PK is cheap here.
    9. Merge Join (Customer)Physical Merge Join. Logical Inner JoinAttach c.Name. Same idea: sorted on CustomerId, keep matches.
    #Operator (your shot)CostWhy it is expensive
    1Clustered Index Scan OrderLine49%Reads 150,000 lines. COUNT(*) has no WHERE on OrderLine, so every line page is touched. Biggest I/O.
    2Clustered Index Scan Orders19%Walks CX_Orders. YEAR(CreatedUtc) is residual — cannot Seek a date. Filter after reading many order rows (~3,889 estimated, ~3,131 kept).
    3Merge Join (Orders + lines)13%Joins ~50k order-counts to ~3k orders. CPU to walk two sorted streams and keep matches.
    4Stream Aggregate9%Groups 150,000 lines into ~50,000 counts — that is COUNT_BIG(*).
    5Sort7%Re-orders ~3,131 rows by CustomerId so the next Merge Join can run.
    6Merge Join (Customer) + Customer scan1% + 1%Customer is only 2,000 rows. Cheap attach of Name.
    —SELECT0%Just the output node. Cost sits on the workers above.
    Who costs most?ImproveWhat will happen
    OrderLine scan 49%You still need line counts. Optional: index/filter on OrderLine only if the query filters lines. Do not “fix” a required count with NOLOCK.Often stays a scan of lines. That is honest work for COUNT(*).
    Orders scan 19% + YEAR residualRewrite: CreatedUtc >= @from AND CreatedUtc < @to. Then index (Status, CreatedUtc) INCLUDE (CustomerId, Total)Predicate on YEAR goes away. Seek/range on Open + this year. Fewer than 3,889 rows touched if most orders are old.

    No Key Lookup here. Clustered scans already have every column. Lookup appears when you Seek a narrow NCI and still need extra columns (steps 7–8).

    Yes — change the query first. An index cannot Seek through YEAR(CreatedUtc). Same meaning: “this calendar year” = from 1 Jan this year up to (not including) 1 Jan next year.

    -- BAD — function on the column (residual, no date Seek) AND YEAR(o.CreatedUtc) = YEAR(SYSUTCDATETIME()) -- GOOD — range on the column (Seek / range possible) AND o.CreatedUtc >= @from AND o.CreatedUtc < @to

    Then Ctrl+M again. Hover the Orders operator: Predicate should be a range on CreatedUtc, not YEAR. OrderLine may still be ~49% — that is the line count, not a failure of this rewrite. After the range looks right, add (Status, CreatedUtc) INCLUDE (CustomerId, Total) if Orders still scans.

    Takeaway: Hover 49% first (OrderLine), then Orders Predicate (YEAR is residual). Missing index is a hint. Rewrite the date first, then index Status + CreatedUtc.

  • Step 15 — OR vs UNION ALL (your shot)

    Open visual guide OR vs UNION ALL. Index in the plan is IX_Orders_Status_Created (key = Status, CreatedUtc). Hover both sides.

    OR (left)UNION ALL (right)
    ShapeOne Index Scan 100%Concatenation: Scan 81% + Index Seek 9%
    Predicate / SeekResidual: CustomerId = 42 OR Status = 'Hold'Top: residual CustomerId = 42. Bottom: Seek Predicates Status = 'Hold'
    Rows read50,000 → 5,025 outScan still 50,000 → 25. Seek 5,000 → 5,000. Concat = 5,025

    Which operator Seeks? Only the bottom branch: WHERE Status = 'Hold'. The index is IX_Orders_Status_Created (Status, CreatedUtc) — leading key = Status, so SQL can jump to Hold. The top branch is WHERE CustomerId = 42. CustomerId is not the key of this index, so that branch still scans. INCLUDE / CreatedUtc do not make a Seek on CustomerId.

    How to improve further: keep UNION ALL (so each filter can Seek), and give the first branch an index on CustomerId — you already have IX_Orders_Customer_Status from Step 1, or follow the green ~88% hint. Then hover: two Index Seeks (25 + 5,000), no 50k scan. If the optimizer still scans, hint/force is last resort — first check both indexes exist and stats are current.

    Takeaway: Verdict: not faster here. Next: UNION ALL + Seek on CustomerId as well as Status.

  • Step 16 — How to read the plan — Microsoft + Fritchey

    Official: Display an Actual Execution Plan. Query → Include Actual Execution Plan (Ctrl+M) → Execute → Execution Plan tab.

    OrderLook for
    1. SELECT nodeFritchey: warnings, sniffing, missing index
    2. Highest cost %Step 0: Table Scan on Orders — then hover it
    3. ObjectHeap = table name only. Index = index name on that operator
    4. Predicate vs Seek PredicatesSeek Predicates = jump using the key. Residual Predicate = check later (on a scan, or on Key Lookup if the column is not in the NCI)
    5. Output ListColumns emitted. Extra columns not in the index → Key Lookup
    5b. Nested Loops / Inner JoinPhysical = method (one by one). Logical = result (keep the pair). You did not write a JOIN. Outer References = OrderId
    6. Rows Read vs Actual RowsTouched vs kept. Read ≫ actual = residual after a scan/seek
    7. Fat arrowMany rows moving to the next operator (actual rows, not rows read)
    8. Estimated vs actual rowsOff by 10× → stats / sniffing
    9. Operator nameTable Scan / CI Scan / Seek / Key Lookup / Hash Match

    Estimated = Ctrl+L (no run). Tune from actual.

    Takeaway: SELECT first, then the 100% operator. Hover Object, Predicate, Output List, then Rows Read vs Actual Rows. Cost % is not a stopwatch.

Interview — questions & answers

Q: Estimated vs actual plan?

A: Estimated is Ctrl+L — guess, no run. Actual is Ctrl+M then Execute. I tune from actual on MyDB.

Q: Why is Orders a heap?

A: No clustered index. Seed CREATE TABLE had no PRIMARY KEY CLUSTERED. Object Explorer Indexes is empty. HEAP + WHERE CustomerId/Status → Table Scan of 50,000 rows. We left it that way on purpose.

Q: What did step 0 show?

A: Table Scan. Object = dbo.Orders (no index name). Predicate = CustomerId and Status residual. Output List = the SELECT columns. Rows read 50,000, actual rows 0 — WHERE did not skip I/O.

Q: Rows read 50,000 — is that the only number?

A: No. Pair it with Actual Number of Rows (0). Object / Predicate / Output List say what, which filter, which columns. Estimated rows is a guess. Cost % is not time.

Q: After CX_Orders, why still a scan?

A: Clustered key is OrderId. Filter is CustomerId/Status. Object = CX_Orders, operator = Clustered Index Scan, still 50,000 rows read. Seek needs NCI on the WHERE columns.

Q: Key columns vs INCLUDE?

A: Key = WHERE — SQL uses them to find matching rows, like the index at the back of a book. INCLUDE = SELECT — stored with the index so SQL can return those values without going back to the main table. Not for searching.

Q: What is in the NCI leaf? When is Key Lookup?

A: Leaf stores key (CustomerId, Status), INCLUDE columns, and OrderId. Seek uses CustomerId/Status. If SELECT needs a column not in that leaf (CreatedUtc when INCLUDE is only Total), Nested Loops Inner Join drives a Key Lookup on OrderId into CX_Orders.

Q: Nested Loops vs Inner Join on the lookup plan?

A: Same operator, two names. Physical Nested Loops = the method: for each of the 25 Seek rows, look up that OrderId. Logical Inner Join = the result: keep the pair (Seek columns + CreatedUtc). I did not write a JOIN — SQL added it to fetch the missing column.

Q: WHERE Status if Status is not in the NCI key?

A: Seek uses only CustomerId — 25 rows. Status is residual on Key Lookup: 25 read, 19 kept, 6 dropped. Key Lookup is ~96% of cost. Put Status in the key → Seek 19, 19 lookups. Also INCLUDE CreatedUtc → Seek only, no lookup.

Q: Always avoid Key Lookup?

A: No. Hover Number of Executions. Many lookups on a hot query → INCLUDE. A few lookups, or a wide rare column → covering can cost more on writes. Here 25 lookups at 96% — I cover.

Q: YEAR() join plan — what do you hover?

A: Highest cost first: OrderLine CI Scan 49% (150k lines for COUNT). Then Orders CI Scan Predicate — YEAR(CreatedUtc) is residual, so no date Seek. Merge Join = both sides sorted on OrderId. Green missing index is a hint; rewrite the date first.

Q: Do you fix YEAR() with an index or change the query?

A: Change the query first. YEAR vs range: same 3,131 rows, Orders still scans. Then IX_Orders_Status_Created: Orders 20% CI Scan → 1% Seek. OrderLine COUNT can stay ~50–63%.

Q: OR vs UNION ALL — always cheaper?

A: Not in this shot. Verdict: rewrite did not improve — est. 0.23 → 0.28, still 50k read on CustomerId. Keep UNION ALL and Seek CustomerId (IX_Orders_Customer_Status or the 88% hint) so both branches Seek.

Q: YEAR() plan — cost descending?

A: OrderLine scan 49% (150k lines). Orders scan 19% (YEAR residual). Merge Join 13%. Stream Aggregate 9%. Sort 7%. Customer join/scan 1%. SELECT 0%.

Q: Table Scan vs Clustered Index Scan vs Seek?

A: Same WHERE: heap Table Scan 50k read / 25 out; CX Clustered Index Scan still 50k / 25; covering NCI Index Seek 25 / 25. Seek Predicate vs residual Predicate. Cost ~0.24 vs ~0.003.

Q: How do you change a Scan to a Seek?

A: Index key = the WHERE, left to right. No YEAR on the column — use a date range. Matching types. OR may need UNION ALL plus an index per filter. Then create the index. Seekable query with no index still scans.

Q: How many clustered vs nonclustered indexes?

A: Clustered: one or none. None = heap. One because the clustered index is the table — one physical order. Nonclustered: many (SQL Server up to 999). Each extra NCI costs writes. Indexes are B-trees, not binary trees. A heap is not a tree.

Q: How do you fix the join query?

A: Stop YEAR(CreatedUtc). Use a date range. Match varchar to 'Open', not 1. Optional index (Status, CreatedUtc).

Slide 17 of 21 · C5 — Microservices & AWS
Microservices, Saga, CQRS
What this primarily describes: Microservices, Saga, CQRS — How many services, how they talk, transactions across services.

Definition

A microservice is a separately deployed API with its own data. Saga = a story of local commits plus undo if a later step fails (no one SQL transaction across HTTP). CQRS = Command Query Responsibility Segregation — write model vs read model. Only say it if you had that split.
  • What it is: Split by domain (orders vs auth vs catalog). Sync = HTTP when the caller needs the answer now. Async = queue when work can wait. Saga = compensate, not BEGIN TRAN across services. CQRS = separate read store.
  • How you use it: User GET = HTTP + service token (client credentials) or mTLS. Email/search = SQS. After local SaveChanges, publish a small event. Fat payload → S3 + key on the message. Failed consumer: retry, then DLQ.
  • Purpose / impact: Purpose: auth/users not copied into every database; scale writes and reads apart if you need it. Impact: one giant SQL transaction across HTTP → locks and timeouts. Silent fail on the queue → lost email. 10MB on the bus → rejected. Name CQRS with no read store → they drill you.
  • Service token: Service-to-service uses client credentials or mTLS — not the user’s browser JWT forwarded forever. Incoming user JWT can be exchanged for a short-lived service token.

    // Order service — local ACID, then publish await _db.SaveChangesAsync(); // local transaction committed await _bus.Publish(new OrderPlaced(order.Id)); // next hop (Inventory, Payment) // Inventory fails → compensating event, not ROLLBACK on Order’s SQL await _bus.Publish(new OrderFailed(order.Id)); // Order handler: status = Cancelled (compensate) // Fat payload: S3 + key on the message (bus size limits) await _s3.PutAsync($"orders/{id}.json", body); await _bus.Publish(new OrderPlaced(id, s3Key: $"orders/{id}.json"));

Show answer
Explains sync vs async, service token, and one reason for Saga or CQRS
Interview — questions & answers

Q: How do microservices communicate? Service-to-service auth?

A: Sync: HTTP with a service token (client credentials) or mTLS. Async: SQS/SNS/Rabbit. Incoming user JWT is not blindly forwarded forever — short-lived or exchanged.

Q: Failed consumer?

A: Retry with backoff, then dead-letter. Alert. Idempotent handler so a retry does not double-charge.

Q: Why CQRS / Saga in your project?

A: Only if we had separate read store or a multi-step business flow. If we did not, I say we used a modular monolith / single DB transaction and I know when I would introduce saga.

Q: 10MB+ event payload?

A: Bus limits. Put the body in S3 and send the object key on the message.

AWS practical
What this primarily describes: AWS practical — Purpose of each service you used — 2026 expects hands-on, not a list.

Definition

AWS here means one path you built, not a service list. Example: Angular on S3, API on ECS behind an ALB, image in ECR. 2026 expects hands-on: containers, how you scale, how you cut cost.
  • What it is: ALB = Application Load Balancer (HTTP to ECS). API Gateway = HTTP front door + authorizer. NLB = Network Load Balancer (TCP / static IP). ECR = Elastic Container Registry (Docker image). ECS = Elastic Container Service (runs tasks). S3 = Simple Storage Service (files / SPA).
  • How you use it: CI: publish → docker build → push ECR → ECS rolling deploy. ALB 443 → target group /health. Angular: ng build → s3 sync → CloudFront. Secrets in SSM/Secrets Manager, not in the image. Scale ECS on CPU or queue depth; scale in at night.
  • Purpose / impact: Purpose: put the API on a URL, store the image, host the SPA, not pay peak 24/7. Impact: laundry list (EKS, Glue, Athena…) you never used → they pick one and you freeze. Idle extra NAT/ALB → bill. Secrets in the image → leaked.
  • Scale & cost: Add tasks when CPU or SQS depth rises; scale in at night. Spot for retryable workers. S3 lifecycle. Turn off idle non-prod. Do not pay peak 24/7.

Interview — questions & answers

Q: Which AWS services and why?

A: Answer with purpose: ALB routes HTTP to tasks, ECR stores the image, S3 holds files, SQS decouples email. Skip unused logos.

Q: ALB vs NLB?

A: ALB: HTTP path/host, WAF, target group health. NLB: TCP/TLS, extreme throughput, static IPs.

Q: How do you scale? How do you cut a high bill with variable traffic?

A: Auto-scale ECS/SQS. Scheduled scale-in. Right-size. Spot for workers if we can retry. S3 lifecycle. Turn off idle non-prod.

Q: Where is the Docker image deployed? Spin containers?

A: Push to ECR. ECS task definition references the image tag. Service keeps N tasks healthy in the cluster/VPC.

Slide 19 of 21 · C6 — Scenarios & legacy
Behavioral and AI scenarios
What this primarily describes: Behavioral and AI scenarios — Repeated four: delay, PR conflict, priorities, AI assistant.

Definition

Behavioral here is what you did, not a slogan. Same four scenes in several 2026 sessions: delay, PR conflict, priorities, AI assistant — plus a schema sketch. They hire people who escalate early and do not rubber-stamp a bad PR.
  • What it is: Delay = risk to a date. PR conflict = review disagreement. Priorities = more than one “number one.” AI = a coding assistant you still own. Plus they liked an orders schema with transactional stock.
  • How you use it: Delay: same day, impact + options (scope / date / help) + a new date. Security/data bugs: do not approve. Style: team standard. Priorities: one ranking written down. AI: name the tool, small diffs, tests, no secrets in chat.

Interview — questions & answers

Q: Unable to complete in the expected timeline — how do you tell your manager?

A: Early, with facts: what's done, blocker, options, ask for a decision. Offer a smaller shippable slice.

Q: Teammate refuses review comments — still approve?

A: Not if it is correctness, security, or supportability. If it is style, I link the guideline. I don't fight taste; I don't merge known bugs.

Q: Which AI coding agent and how do you keep quality?

A: I name one I actually use. Constraints in the prompt, small diffs, tests, no secrets in chat, I still understand every line I commit.

Slide 20 of 21 · C6 — Scenarios & legacy
Legacy IIS / ASP.NET extras
What this primarily describes: Legacy IIS / ASP.NET extras — Second flavour: manual IIS, WebForms, SP walkthrough, prod RCA without access.

Definition

The legacy IIS track still asks how you run an old ASP.NET site by hand: app pools, recycle, WebForms postback, cookies, and a production issue with no prod access. Same JWT questions sit on top. iisreset is the big hammer — it restarts every site on the box.
  • What it is: Application pool = worker process + identity for one or more apps. iisreset = restart ALL IIS sites. Recycle = one pool. WebForms = postback, ViewState, page lifecycle. RCA = Root Cause Analysis.
  • How you use it: One pool per site. Deploy: stop pool, copy files, start pool. Logs: IIS W3SVC + app + Event Viewer. No prod: staging SP + ticket parameters. ADO/Dapper for heavy SPs; EF for CRUD. Be ready to read a 100-line SP out loud.
  • Purpose / impact: Purpose: change one site without killing the box; find a bug without guessing. Impact: iisreset on a shared server → every site down. “I need prod” with no log story → they stop. Cookie vs JWT: this track still asks tamper/expiry.
  • ADO vs EF: ADO/Dapper for heavy stored procedures; EF for CRUD. Be ready to walk a long SP line by line.

Interview — questions & answers

Q: What is an application pool? What happens on iisreset?

A: Pool = worker process identity + recycling settings for one or more apps. iisreset stops IIS — all sites go down. Prefer pool recycle or a rolling deploy.

Q: Client reported an issue, no prod access — RCA?

A: Collect logs they can export, IIS status codes, correlate by time/request id, run the SP in staging, compare config. Do not guess.

Q: JWT tamper / expiry?

A: Signature check on the API. exp claim. Same as core track — they still ask it on the legacy IIS panel.

Interview — questions & answers

Q: Give the Interview 5 in one breath for DI.

A: DI is the container constructing dependencies. I used it in Program.cs. Why: testable, swap SQL. How: constructor injection, Scoped DbContext. Problem: no new SqlConnection in the controller.

Q: One sentence on CORS.

A: SPA origin differs from API origin; we allowlist the Angular origin and still send the Bearer token on XHR.

Q: Ready?
